title: Audit-grade Real Estate Transaction Deep Insight Framework: For Management Governance
affiliations: The University of Western Australia

detail.title: Audit-grade Real Estate Transaction Deep Insight Framework: For Management Governance
detail.abstract: This paper examines open data on real estate transactions in the US state of Connecticut, integrating drift auditing, quantile-preserving forecasting, transaction-level anomaly detection, and system-level sequential alerting into an auditable chain of evidence. It explores the implications for management governance. Unlike the common 'point prediction-error comparison' approach, this study focuses on questions managers genuinely need to assess in dynamic markets: whether data remains a viable decision baseline, whether models retain interval-level reliability, and whether risk signals can be identified through layered detection. The study employs forward-looking time segmentation: the training period concludes in 2018, the calibration period spans 2019-2020, and the testing period covers 2021-2023. Using 2001-2005 as the drift audit baseline, results indicate that the target variable's overall stability index (PSI_y) increased from 0.2973 to 0.5509, while the overall stability index for the first feature variable (PSI_x1) increased from 0.4413 to 0.6629. This indicates that distribution drift in both the target and feature layers continued to intensify throughout the testing period. Interval prediction results demonstrate that the more concise Spec A achieves both higher coverage and narrower interval width under the current sample, exhibiting relatively more robust interval prediction performance. Anomaly monitoring results further indicate a persistent rise in transaction-level anomaly rates. However, both EWMA and CUSUM exhibit low detection rates and prolonged median delays, revealing a significant time lag between local anomaly increases and system-level confirmation. The managerial significance of this paper lies in transforming real estate forecasting into a governance problem. It replaces singular precision-oriented approaches with mechanism distinguishability and evidence verifiability, explicitly preserving the unclosed boundaries of the interpretive layer.

title: Agentic Workflow Drift and Agentic Workflow Subversion: A New Risk Taxonomy for the Governance of Agentic AI in Financial Services

detail.title: Agentic Workflow Drift and Agentic Workflow Subversion: A New Risk Taxonomy for the Governance of Agentic AI in Financial Services

detail.abstract:
Banks are beginning to deploy AI systems that do not just automate decisions — they determine whether decisions should be made at all. As agentic AI moves into workflow orchestration, a new failure mode is emerging workflows that execute correctly against definitions that were never explicitly authorized.

This paper introduces two original concepts: Agentic Workflow Drift and Agentic Workflow Subversion. Drift occurs when agentic systems reconcile inconsistent definitions across enterprise platforms into a working logic that no human explicitly approved. Subversion is the enterprise risk surface that emerges when this drift propagates across workflows, or is deliberately exploited by sophisticated actors, without triggering existing detection frameworks.

The paper argues that this risk originates in a previously ungoverned layer of enterprise architecture: the reasoning layer, where meaning is resolved before execution proceeds. Existing governance frameworks in financial services, including model risk management, controls testing, and operational risk, were not designed to govern this layer directly or comprehensively.

Using a detailed banking example spanning KYC, credit, and entitlement systems, the paper demonstrates how semantically inconsistent definitions can be synthesized into an unauthorized operating logic that propagates silently across workflows while all controls appear to function as designed. Cyber sees no breach. Fraud sees no misuse. Model risk sees no statistical deviation. The result is not control failure. It is valid execution against shifted meaning.

To address this gap, the paper proposes the Semantic Control Plane, a governance architecture that enforces consistent definitions at runtime before agentic reasoning determines execution. It further introduces the Agentic 3 C's Framework, comprising Context, Control, and Coordination, as the operating principles required to make agentic AI governable at enterprise scale.

Drawing on practitioner expertise in banking controls, model risk governance, and enterprise architecture, this work contributes what is, to the author's knowledge, the first risk taxonomy developed specifically for the reasoning layer of agentic AI systems in financial services, reframing AI risk from model outputs to the governance of meaning itself.

The Age of Inference is here. Banks that fail to govern the reasoning layer will not fail loudly. They will fail invisibly, within systems that appear fully controlled.

title: When the Perfect is the Enemy of the Good: Price Discrimination, Affordability, Precarity and Market Dynamism

detail.title: When the Perfect is the Enemy of the Good: Price Discrimination, Affordability, Precarity and Market Dynamism
detail.abstract: Price discrimination is facing growing consumer and regulatory backlash due to the emergence of "surveillance pricing," which uses personal data to set individualized prices. Machine learning algorithms draw on a customer's purchase history, location, demographic characteristics, credit information, and even cursor movements or inferred emotional states to estimate willingness to pay with unprecedented precision, bringing markets closer to the theoretical case of perfect price discrimination. The resulting transfer of surplus from consumers to firms raises issues that extend beyond traditional analyses of price discrimination. Personalized pricing has implications not only for market efficiency but also for income distribution, social norms of fairness, the transparency of price signals, and international economic relations when surplus is extracted by globally headquartered digital platforms. These concerns stretch the limits of the conventional analytical framework, which evaluates price discrimination primarily through the lens of consumer surplus in a partial-equilibrium setting. As authorities worldwide confront the regulatory challenges posed by algorithmic pricing, greater conceptual ambition is called for: the longstanding view that imperfect price discrimination can enhance welfare may not survive when markets approach the theoretical limit of perfect price discrimination.

title: The Vertical Fiscal Ratchet: Asymmetric State Tax Responses to Federal Tax Changes Over 100 Years

detail.title: The Vertical Fiscal Ratchet: Asymmetric State Tax Responses to Federal Tax Changes Over 100 Years
detail.abstract: Do federal tax cuts reduce the overall tax burden? Using a century-long panel of 48 continental U.S. states (1910-2022) across five tax types, I document a fundamental asymmetry in vertical fiscal interactions: states do not follow federal tax increases but actively raise their own rates when federal rates decline. This vertical fiscal ratchet is three to four times larger for federal decreases than increases and is consistent across personal income, corporate income, tobacco, gasoline, and spirit taxes. I introduce three pre-tax-era exposure measures, predetermined by geography and early industrialization, that extend causal identification of vertical fiscal interactions to the personal income tax for the first time. Controlling for horizontal competition through neighbor-state taxes does not eliminate the asymmetric effect, resolving a challenge posed by Devereux et al. (2007). These findings reconcile contradictory results in prior work: the "positive" vertical interaction documented by Besley and Rosen (1998) is driven entirely by state responses to federal retreats, while the near-zero response to federal advances pulls symmetric estimates toward zero. The vertical fiscal ratchet is a mechanism through which federal tax cuts fail to reduce the combined tax burden borne by citizens.

title: The Impact of Stablecoins on the International Monetary and Financial System
affiliations: Bank for International Settlements (BIS), Bank for International Settlements and Portland State University - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Impact of Stablecoins on the International Monetary and Financial System
detail.abstract: Widespread use of stablecoins could have an important impact on the international monetary and financial system, particularly for emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs). Analysing their effect through the framework of international currency functions, we argue that stablecoins are most likely to affect private-sector store of value and medium of exchange roles, particularly in economies facing macroeconomic instability. Given that approximately 98% of stablecoin value is dollar-denominated, they are likely to initially reinforce existing currency hierarchies. We develop three scenarios to explore the range of potential outcomes. In niche adoption, impacts remain contained within crypto ecosystems. Digital dollarisation poses acute risks to monetary sovereignty in EMDEs through rapid currency substitution. Domestic stablecoin integration could harness efficiency gains while preserving policy autonomy, but it requires significant regulatory capacity. The ultimate trajectory will depend on adoption patterns, regulatory responses and the interplay with other forms of digital money.

How to measure the effectiveness of corporate strategies for sustainable development? Moreover, what could engaged IB scholarship focus on in their research and teaching? Why is SDG 8 (decent work and economic growth) thereby particularly relevant? Are we on course?

title: Temporalities of Collapse: Superposed Futures, Soft Attractors, and the Governance of Premature Convergence
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Temporalities of Collapse: Superposed Futures, Soft Attractors, and the Governance of Premature Convergence
detail.abstract: Scenario planning gave the futures field its defining methodology: hold multiple futures simultaneously, prepare for each, predict none. This paper argues that plurality, as currently practiced, is incomplete. Plural-but-separated futures, discrete possibility states inhabited sequentially, still function as premature convergence. Each scenario is a hard attractor. Institutional attention collapses toward it, one future at a time. What the field has not yet built is the capacity to hold futures in genuine superposition: simultaneously operative, without sequential collapse, generating directionality without deterministic commitment. This paper introduces the Superposed Futures as Soft Attractors (SFSA), a formal architecture for anticipatory governance under genuine superposition. The SFSA proposes the probability simplex as the geometry of the currently reachable possibility space, bounded by path dependency rather than imagination. Soft attractors tilt this space toward certain futures without eliminating others. An openness governance parameter determines how much concentration is permitted before event-time conditions warrant it. The anti-collapse property of the architecture ensures no future is permanently foreclosed while openness remains active. Anticipatory governance is reconceived from preparedness-for-futures to operability-under-superposition. The distinction between clock-time and event-time governance identifies the mechanism by which premature collapse most commonly occurs in institutional practice. Three types of event-time condition are defined and distinguished. The path-dependent and irreversible character of weight concentration establishes why the timing of collapse carries asymmetric governance stakes.

title: Artificial Influence: How AI Role and Gender Reshape Team Dynamics
affiliations: University of Notre Dame, University of Notre Dame, University of Notre Dame - Department of Management & Administration Sciences and University of Notre Dame

detail.title: Artificial Influence: How AI Role and Gender Reshape Team Dynamics
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly embedded directly within organizational teams, where they advise, coordinate, and shape collective decisions. As a result, organizations must decide not only whether to deploy AI but also how AI should participate in team interactions. We examine how two common design choices, the role assigned to an AI system (advisor versus assistant) and its gendered presentation (male versus female), shape both human interaction with AI and the dynamics between human team members. Across two studies using an incentivized investment task, we show that these design choices systematically shape both reliance on AI input and the dynamics that emerge within teams. Study 1 isolates individual decision making and shows that AI role and gender affect reliance on AI advice and investment behavior. Study 2 embeds the AI within three-person teams interacting in virtual reality, allowing fine-grained behavioral measurement of gaze, communication, and decision responsibility. We find that AI design choices reshape when AI is used, how teams interact, and who ultimately drives decisions, revealing spillover effects on human-human interaction beyond the immediate human-AI exchange. These results demonstrate that AI is not merely a decision aid but a social actor whose design can redistribute influence and alter team dynamics.

title: Regulating AI Agents
affiliations: The Future Society, The Future Society and Hebrew University of Jerusalem

detail.title: Regulating AI Agents
detail.abstract: AI agents—systems that can independently take actions to pursue complex goals with only limited human oversight—have entered the mainstream. These systems are now being widely used to produce software, conduct business activities, and automate everyday personal tasks. While AI agents implicate many areas of law, ranging from agency law and contracts to tort liability and labor law, they present particularly pressing questions for the most globally consequential AI regulation: the European Union’s AI Act. Promulgated prior to the development and widespread use of AI agents, the EU AI Act faces significant obstacles in confronting the governance challenges arising from this transformative technology, such as performance failures in autonomous task execution, the risk of misuse of agents by malicious actors, and unequal access to the economic opportunities afforded by AI agents. We systematically analyze the EU AI Act’s response to these challenges, focusing on both the substantive provisions of the regulation and, crucially, the institutional frameworks that aim to support its implementation. Our analysis of the Act’s allocation of monitoring and enforcement responsibilities, reliance on industry self-regulation, and level of government resourcing illustrates how a regulatory framework designed for conventional AI systems can be ill-suited to AI agents. Taken together, our findings suggest that policymakers in the EU and beyond will need to change course, and soon, if they are to effectively govern the next generation of AI technology.

title: Knowledge Sharing in Networked Communities of Practice: Computational Network Analysis of Organizing Dynamics in Online Crowdsourcing Communities
affiliations: Syracuse University

detail.title: Knowledge Sharing in Networked Communities of Practice: Computational Network Analysis of Organizing Dynamics in Online Crowdsourcing Communities

publicationDetails.detailsText: accepted by Computers in Human Behavior

detail.abstract: This study examines the knowledge-sharing dynamics of crowdsourcing challenge communities (CCCs), conceptualized as possessing the hybrid features of both communities of practice (CoPs) and networks of practice (NoPs). A systematic review on CoPs and NoPs points toward the rarity of longitudinal network analysis within the area and the risks of overlooking the impact of external groups of the communities. Addressing these gaps, this research identifies several different types of reciprocity patterns in the communities using longitudinal network analyses (i.e., relational event modeling). Results suggest CCCs are competitive and temporary challenge communities. Idea innovators contribute until they receive communication ties from others. Their contribution is also dominated by direct reciprocity (which means favor is being directly returned to the original sender), reflecting the potentially self-interested culture of the communities. Visitors, temporary participants who do not directly compete in the challenges but share comments, were found to have a significant impact on encouraging the knowledge-exchange norms of the community members. Managers' impact was also significant in improving knowledge sharing. In practice, the management of online CCCs should be aware that networked communities of practice are still egocentric, and community-oriented norms are largely lacking, which is nurturing because support is often conditional and self-serving and may risk the loss of community members over time. This paper contributes to the practice community (i.e., CoP and NoP) literature by recognizing the hybridity of CCCs. This paper also contributes to the synthesis and development of network reciprocity and the evolution of knowledge sharing networks.

title: Stablecoin Yield, Shadow Banking, and the Myth of "Necessary" Rewards
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: Stablecoin Yield, Shadow Banking, and the Myth of "Necessary" Rewards
detail.abstract: The debate over the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act (GENIUS Act) has quickly evolved beyond its formal text into a broader policy claim: that the United States must permit interest and "rewards" on stablecoins to foster innovation and remain competitive with foreign digital asset regimes. 1 Proponents, such as Guiterrez, argue that prohibiting yield on payment stablecoins will entrench incumbent banks, suppress consumer returns, and hand a strategic advantage to offshore stablecoins and foreign central bank digital currencies. 2 This essay takes that claim seriously but contends that it is both overstated and conceptually confused. Properly understood, yield on stablecoins is not a free lunch of innovation, but a design choice that reintroduces the familiar problems of shadow banking, regulatory arbitrage, and run risk in a new technological wrapper.

title: Pressure of Quality, and Quality under Pressure: The Psychology and Economics of Diligence in America
affiliations: University of Erfurt

detail.title: Pressure of Quality, and Quality under Pressure: The Psychology and Economics of Diligence in America
detail.abstract: We study attitudes toward diligence as it relates to quality orientation in the U.S. The concept of diligence aversion captures the burden of having to consistently work toward a high standard of output quality. We conducted a survey that offers insights into drivers of diligence aversion like the experienced quality pressure, the pride a person takes producing high quality, and the expectations of changing demands for diligence. We further investigate an age effect thatwhen comparing international data-hints at a trend toward higher diligence aversion in the U.S. Drawing on additional forms of evidence we identify tendencies both for declining diligence as well as organizational efforts to sustain it.

title: Commercial Paper Markets in Crisis: A Comparative Review of Systemic Fragility, Central Bank Intervention, and Market Design Across Episodes (1970-2020)
affiliations: IIM Kozhikode

detail.title: Commercial Paper Markets in Crisis: A Comparative Review of Systemic Fragility, Central Bank Intervention, and Market Design Across Episodes (1970-2020)
detail.abstract: Commercial paper (CP) markets occupy a structural node in the modern financial system, channelling short-term credit to corporations, financial intermediaries, and government-sponsored enterprises. Yet their hallmark properties-ultra-short maturities, continuous rollover dependence, and rating-cliff sensitivity-render them disproportionately fragile relative to their apparent simplicity. This systematic review synthesises scholarship spanning five decades to construct the first unified analytical framework encompassing all four systemic CP market disruptions: the Penn Central default of 1970, the asset-backed commercial paper (ABCP) conduit crisis of August 2007, the broad CP market freeze following Lehman Brothers' collapse in September 2008, and the COVID-19 liquidity shock of March 2020. Drawing on empirical and theoretical studies from leading economics and finance journals, we argue that while the surface triggers differed dramatically across episodesa railroad insolvency, structured-finance unravelling, counterparty fear, and pandemic panic-the underlying vulnerability was constant: maturity mismatch between rolled-over short-term liabilities and illiquid or informationally opaque underlying assets. We document how the Federal Reserve's lender-of-last-resort posture evolved from informal moral suasion (1970) through the Commercial Paper Funding Facility (2008) to near-instantaneous reactivation (2020), each cycle deepening implicit public support for private money markets. This trajectory creates a paradox: each intervention reduced immediate systemic cost yet reinforced structural fragility by subsidising continued reliance on wholesale short-term funding. We identify three active research gaps: the net redistribution effect of post-2016 money market fund reforms; the boundary between credit and liquidity interventions; and the emerging nexus between stablecoin growth and CP demand dynamics.

title: Exploiting common volatility dynamics in high-dimensional portfolio selection
affiliations: University of Regensburg and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Exploiting common volatility dynamics in high-dimensional portfolio selection
detail.abstract: We develop a framework for forecasting high-dimensional covariance matrices for portfolio selection that exploits comovement in monthly realized volatilities. We consider factor models and pooled autoregressive moving average (ARMA) models with parameters constrained within pre-specified groups of stocks. We establish a formal link between the two modeling approaches by showing that a pooled ARMA model admits a dynamic factor representation and can be understood as a static factor model with group-specific factors. Volatility forecasts are combined with (realized-)dynamic conditional correlation (DCC) estimates to obtain conditional covariance matrices, which are evaluated in a minimum variance portfolio selection setting. For portfolios constructed from S&P 500 constituents, our best-performing approach pools volatility dynamics across the entire cross-section. We find that this approach outperforms the unconditional covariance estimate obtained via nonlinear shrinkage by 20.2% in terms of annualized portfolio standard deviation. This strong performance is further supported by comparisons with competing conditional covariance estimators as well as extensive robustness checks.

title: Estimating the Impact of Industrial Catches on the Productivity of Artisanal Fishers in Senegal
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Kiel - Institute of Statistics and Econometrics, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Christian-Albrechts-University Kiel - Faculty of Agricultural and Nutritional Sciences & Center for Ocean and Society

detail.title: Estimating the Impact of Industrial Catches on the Productivity of Artisanal Fishers in Senegal
detail.abstract: As global fish stocks face increasing pressure from overfishing, competition between industrial and artisanal fishers is intensifying. This study aims to quantify the impact of industrial fishing on the productivity of artisanal fishers in Senegal. To examine this, monthly data collected from quantitative interviews with 134 artisanal fishers was combined with official artisanal catch data and Global Fishing Watch records on industrial fishing effort. Given the unavailability of direct biomass estimates on a monthly scale, we derive a theory-based proxy based on a combination of monthly sea surface temperature with overall monthly catches and yearly controls for long-term stock trends. Results based on fixed-effects regression indicate competition for resources among small artisanal crews and between large artisanal crews and the industrial fleet. An increase in industrial catches significantly reduces the productivity of large artisanal crews. For large artisanal boats, a 100 ton increase in industrial catches results in approximately 5.3 USD in lost revenue per fisher per month, which is equivalent to two thirds of daily median agricultural wage in the region. Overall, a decline in productivity of the artisanal fleet was evident during the study period. In addition to policies addressing the overall decline in productivity, which may be linked to ecosystem degradation, improved fishery management (e.g. efficient allocation of fishing quotas) has the potential to stabilize productivity by fostering healthier ecosystems, and to mitigate excessive competition through clearer allocation of resources. This is essential to ensure food security and safeguard the livelihoods of local fishers.

title: Impact of Financial Development on Industrial R&D: Evidence from OECD Countries
affiliations: University of Wisconsin - Milwaukee and University of Wisconsin - Milwaukee

detail.title: Impact of Financial Development on Industrial R&D: Evidence from OECD Countries
detail.abstract: Whether financial development promotes industrial innovation depends not just on how developed a country's financial system is, but on which dimensions of that system are well developed. This paper examines how depth, access, and efficiency of both financial institutions and financial markets shape R&D investment across industries that differ in their reliance on external finance. Using industrylevel data from the ISIC Rev. 4 classification across 18 OECD countries from 1995 to 2019, and drawing on the IMF's multidimensional Financial Development Index, we analyze how country-level financial development measures interact with an industry-level external finance dependence measure to influence R&D intensity measured relative to output and value added. Our findings show that the overall level of financial development matters primarily through depth. In particular, the depth of financial institutions and, to a lesser extent, the depth of financial markets significantly raise R&D intensity in industries that depend more heavily on external funding. Measures of access and efficiency display little systematic effect. The results are strongest within manufacturing industries, where innovation activity is concentrated. These findings highlight the importance of financial structure and, in particular, the scale and capacity of financial intermediation, in shaping the allocation of innovative investment across industries.

title: Extending Transaction Cost Economics to AI/Cloud Ecosystems

detail.title: Extending Transaction Cost Economics to AI/Cloud Ecosystems
detail.abstract: Organizations increasingly rely on artificial intelligence and cloud ecosystems to deliver strategic value, yet many AI/Cloud initiatives experience governance failures involving vendor lock-in, regulatory non-compliance, and unrealized initiative outcomes. This paper extends Transaction Cost Economics (TCE) by introducing Digital Transaction Hazards (DTH)a formative composite of Algorithmic Uncertainty, Dynamic Ecosystem Specificity, and Regulatory Volatility and proposing a four-construct, capability-mediated governance model: AI/Cloud Governance Capability (ACGC) enables Safeguarding Mechanisms (SM) deployment (β1 > 0), which attenuates DTH exposure (β2 < 0), which determines AI/Cloud Initiative Success (ACIS) (β3 < 0), with full sequential mediation as the theorized baseline. AI/Cloud ecosystems motivate this extension by violating three structural assumptions of classical TCE: discrete, bounded transactions; bilateral governance relationships; and stable institutional environments. These are not contextual complications-they are boundary conditions under which TCE's original assumptions no longer hold and formal theoretical extension is required. The model reframes Williamson's discriminating alignment principle as a capability-mediated execution problem rather than a governance structure selection problem. It also extends the DeLone and McLean IS Success Model with a Responsible AI Outcomes dimension grounded in TCE ex post cost logic and establishes theoretical lineage from Tran and Guzman (2013). The paper extends TCE's reach from static, dyadic exchange relationships to dynamic, ecosystem-based digital transactionswithout replacing its core efficiency logic.

title: After the AI Crash

detail.title: After the AI Crash
detail.abstract: Trillions of dollars in AI infrastructure investment rest on tens of billions in revenues, and the opaque financial engineering involved—circular equity, off-balance-sheet debt, and distortive subsidies—means a market correction could trigger an economy-wide crash rather than a contained sectoral downturn. This paper describes how such a crash might unfold and proposes several bold policy recommendations for Congress: curtailing risky financial engineering; prosecuting fraud; converting stranded data centers into a public cloud; sustaining public-purpose AI R&D; protecting workers through expanding unemployment insurance, creating a Digital Works Progress Administration, and ending worker surveillance; structurally separating algorithms from infrastructure; regulating digital utilities and establishing a new digital regulator; and banning surveillance-based business models (i.e., ads, pricing, wages).

title: Is Energy Efficiency Contagious? Evidence from Peer Effects in Home Retrofits
affiliations: Hitotsubashi University

detail.title: Is Energy Efficiency Contagious? Evidence from Peer Effects in Home Retrofits
detail.abstract: This paper estimates causal peer effects in residential energy consumption using Canada’s largest home energy efficiency retrofit program. We combine administrative program records with more than a decade of house-level utility data from a mid-sized Canadian city. Our identification strategy exploits spatial variation in retrofit timing and compares houses located near retrofitted homes to those near “almost retrofitted” homes, properties that completed a pre-retrofit energy audit but did not undertake upgrades. Because both groups reveal similar intentions to invest in energy efficiency, this approach mitigates reflection and selection concerns. We find that households reduce natural gas consumption by about 2% and electricity consumption by roughly 1% after a nearby retrofit. These effects persist for more than a decade and are strongest for highly visible upgrades, such as window replacements and exterior wall insulation. The results provide causal evidence of localized social spillovers and suggest that policies promoting visible efficiency investments can amplify the impact of decarbonization programs.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the integration of artificial intelligence-driven predictive maintenance systems with environmental risk analytics in industrial operations, with the aim of improving operational resilience, sustainability, and regulatory compliance. Using a synthesis of empirical findings from prior industrial AI deployments and comparative analysis of predictive modeling frameworks, the study evaluates how machine learning, computer vision, IoT data streams, and environmental modeling can be combined into unified decision-support systems (Adeparusi; Abbas; Ünlü and Söylemez). The findings indicate that integrated AI frameworks significantly reduce unplanned equipment downtime while also improving emissions forecasting, environmental risk anticipation, and sustainability performance (Bello et al.; Ajenifuja and Adeparusi 2024b). However, results also reveal unexpected short-term trade-offs, particularly where maintenance optimization increased localized emissions due to intensified asset utilization (AdeparuBhalani). The study concludes that predictive maintenance systems that exclude environmental analytics risk reinforcing unsustainable industrial practices, while integrated models align more closely with Industry 5.0 principles of responsibility, resilience, and human-centric automation (Ejjami and Boussalham).

title: Scope, Limitations, and Conditions of Application of the Structural Model

detail.title: Scope, Limitations, and Conditions of Application of the Structural Model
detail.abstract: This supplementary paper clarifies the scope, limitations, and conditions of application of the proposed structural model of social behavior. It does not introduce new claims, but aims to prevent misuse and excessive generalization by explicitly distinguishing descriptive analysis from normative or prescriptive interpretation. By specifying analytical boundaries and excluded conditions, this supplement stabilizes the application of the model and reinforces its role as a descriptive framework for understanding patterns of behavior in human society.

title: Hybrid Reliability Models for High-Risk Industrial Processes Incorporating Probabilistic AI

detail.title: Hybrid Reliability Models for High-Risk Industrial Processes Incorporating Probabilistic AI
detail.abstract: This study examines hybrid reliability models for high-risk industrial processes that integrate probabilistic artificial intelligence with established reliability engineering techniques, including Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA), Root Cause Analysis (RCA), and multi-criteria decision-making frameworks. Drawing on evidence from manufacturing, energy, and intelligent production systems, the study synthesizes findings from recent empirical and methodological research to evaluate how probabilistic AI enhances failure prediction, uncertainty handling, and system resilience (Ajenifuja and Adeparusi 2024b; Duan et al.). The results indicate that hybrid models outperform deterministic and single-model AI approaches in anticipating rare events, adapting to dynamic operating conditions, and supporting risk-informed decision-making (Mishra et al.; Chakhrit et al.). However, the analysis also reveals unexpected challenges related to data dependency, computational complexity, and the integration of human factors (Hasan; AdeparuBhalani). The study concludes that probabilistic AI-enabled hybrid reliability models provide a more trustworthy and resilient framework for managing high-risk industrial processes, particularly when aligned with human-centric and sustainability-oriented design principles (Mishra et al.; Adeparusi and Ajenifuja 2025).

title: The Changing Information Content of Options Markets: Evidence from 1996–2024
affiliations: Rutgers Business School - Rutgers University

detail.title: The Changing Information Content of Options Markets: Evidence from 1996–2024
detail.abstract: We examine option-market signals as predictors of stock returns using 8,136 U.S. equities over 1,510 weeks (1996-2024). We report three findings. First, the implied volatility spread remains robust throughout the sample, generating a Carhart four-factor weekly alpha of-29.4 basis points (t =-9.08). Second, the option-to-stock volume ratio (O/S)-which predicted negative returns in the original Johnson and So (2012) sample-has undergone a significant structural break: the predictive sign reverses after 2020 (Chow test p = 0.008). Third, consistent with the short-sale constraint channel, the O/S signal retains predictive power exclusively among stocks with low institutional ownership. We attribute the break to surging retail options participation following the elimination of brokerage commissions in late 2019, which transformed the O/S ratio from an informed-trading indicator into a measure of retail speculative activity.

title: The Effect of Climate Uncertainty on Corporate Investments: R&D vs Capital Expenditure
affiliations: Southern Illinois University Edwardsville - Department of Economics & Finance, SIUE and Penn State Great Valley

detail.title: The Effect of Climate Uncertainty on Corporate Investments: R&D vs Capital Expenditure
detail.abstract: Using 140,478 firm-quarter observations for U.S. firms spanning from 2005 to 2023, we document a significant negative relation between firms' investments in R&D and Capex and their climate risk (or exposure). We find that one standard deviation increase in climate exposure leads to approximately 5% decrease in quarterly R&D investment for an average firm in our sample, double the impact on Capex at 2.56%. We also show that certain firm characteristics mitigate the negative association between climate uncertainty and investments. Particularly, growth prospects offered by firm operations and liquidity conditions help curb the negative effect of climate uncertainty, while firm size and the proportion of tangible assets help mitigate the negative association with R&D. We also find that the asymmetry in the effect of climate uncertainty on Capex and R&D is more pronounced for firms in high climate sensitive industries. These findings suggest that not all investments are alike and the real effect of climate uncertainty on corporate investments critically depends on the type of investment made by firms. The results also suggest that there might be a bright side to climate uncertainty which could help stimulate R&D investments to manage risks associated with climate concerns.

title: Assessing the Benefits of Optimized Agentic AI Systems for Asset Pricing
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Assessing the Benefits of Optimized Agentic AI Systems for Asset Pricing
detail.abstract: Evaluating optimized AI systems for asset pricing is fundamentally difficult for two reasons. First, models are trained on all data, implying that any backtest or analysis using historical data suffers from look-ahead bias. In addition, markets are reflexive-as investors adopt AI, prices adjust-which may erode the very patterns the AI system was trained to exploit. We introduce a real-time, out-of-sample benchmark designed to sidestep both problems. The benchmark measures how well AI systems can explain contemporaneous stock returns around earnings announcements using only information available at announcement time, including the announcement text itself. Applying this benchmark to a range of agentic AI systems-which extract structured signals from earnings call transcripts and optimize over those signals-we find that the best-optimized systems more than double the explained variation in returns relative to standard benchmarks (R 2 increasing from 8% to close to 20%). We also discuss the efficiency gains of AI-based optimization compared to traditional machine learning methods. Beyond predictive performance, these systems generate narrative explanations for price movements that yield testable implications for asset pricing theory. We release an SDK and launch an open competition inviting researchers to improve on our results. Saturating this benchmark would represent fundamental progress in understanding how capital markets process firm-level information.

detail.abstract: This study examines the integration of digital twin technologies within smart factory environments as a mechanism for enhancing environmental resilience and sustainable industrial operations. Drawing on a synthesis of peer-reviewed empirical studies and applied industrial frameworks, the research evaluates how digital twins-when combined with artificial intelligence, industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), and environmental risk analytics-support proactive monitoring, prediction, and mitigation of environmental risks in manufacturing systems (Adeparusi and Ajenifuja; Rahmani et al.). The findings indicate that digital twins significantly improve real-time environmental visibility, predictive risk anticipation, and adaptive response capacity, particularly under conditions of climate variability and operational stress (Ajenifuja and Adeparusi 2024; Bogary). However, the study also identifies unexpected trade-offs, including short-term increases in localized environmental load due to efficiency-driven production intensification (Sahu and Upadhyay). The study concludes that digital twins function not merely as simulation tools but as governance and resilience layers in smart factories, enabling environmentally informed decision-making that aligns operational performance with sustainability objectives (Alnaser et al.; Adeparusi and Ajenifuja 2025).

title: How Well Do Comparable Transaction Filters Predict Biotech Valuations? Evidence from 1,976 Financing Events

detail.title: How Well Do Comparable Transaction Filters Predict Biotech Valuations? Evidence from 1,976 Financing Events

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Venture capital investors and investment banks routinely construct comparable transaction sets by filtering on clinical development stage, therapeutic indication, and drug modality to value biotech companies. Despite the near-universal adoption of this framework, limited empirical evidence supports the assumption that these variables meaningfully predict pre-money valuations. I test this assumption using 1,976 biotech financing transactions spanning 2013 to 2026, sourced from SEC EDGAR filings and cross-referenced with ClinicalTrials.gov for independent clinical taxonomy assignment. I decompose valuation variance using OLS with robust standard errors and Ridge regression with ten-fold cross-validation. The full model — incorporating clinical stage, therapeutic indication, drug modality, deal type, and calendar year — explains approximately 8.8% of log pre-money valuation variance out of sample. The partial 𝑅2 decomposition contradicts conventional practice: deal type contributes 4.2 percentage points, therapeutic indication 1.4, clinical stage 1.2, and drug modality 0.2. Stage — widely treated as the primary valuation driver — ranks third. The stage ladder is largely flat between Phase 1 and Phase 2/3; only Phase 3 companies are reliably distinguishable from Phase 2 firms. The strongest individual effect is a rare disease premium of approximately 3.5 times. When the sample is restricted to IPOs — the transaction type where comparable analyses are most commonly employed — the model’s out-of-sample 𝑅2 turns negative, indicating zero predictive power. These findings suggest that while the comparable transaction framework may serve governance and anchoring functions, it has limited empirical support as a price discovery mechanism for biotech financings.

title: Distance Decay in Online Deliveries and the Sustainability Impact of Pricing Incentives
affiliations: , Imperial College London - Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, , Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and Imperial College London - Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering

detail.title: Distance Decay in Online Deliveries and the Sustainability Impact of Pricing Incentives
detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of last-mile delivery has reshaped urban logistics, yet the spatial patterns governing how delivery flows vary with distance and travel time remain largely unexplored, hindering efficient network design and evidence-based policy interventions. Using a large-scale dataset comprising tens of millions of records from multiple delivery platforms across different continents, we provide a comprehensive empirical estimation of flow-distance relationships in last-mile delivery. Employing semi-parametric spline models and Gaussian process regression, we demonstrate that express delivery orders, including food and grocery, exhibit a universal exponential decay with distance and travel time across all cities. In contrast, centralized scheduled parcel deliveries fulfilled by a small number of peripheral warehouses display near-uniform distance distributions, largely independent of distance. Moreover, we show that pricing mechanisms can meaningfully alter these spatial patterns. In response to delivery fee incentives, customers increase ordering distances by an average of 14%, contradicting the common assumption of treating order travel distance as exogenous. These findings indicate that spatial and environmental externalities are behaviorally responsive to pricing strategies, underscoring the need for interventions that preserve price signals reflecting the true social cost of distance.

title: Shadow Tariffs and the Executive Volatility Regime
affiliations: University of Akron - The George W. Daverio School of Accountancy

detail.title: Shadow Tariffs and the Executive Volatility Regime
detail.abstract: This Article identifies and theorizes a neglected tariff instrument: "shadow tariffs," the tariff-like burdens created by executive volatility rather than by durable border collection. When an administration repeatedly announces, delays, conditions, escalates, and reverses tariffs, it changes the expected distribution of future trade costs. Corporations respond ex ante by repricing risk, rewriting contracts, pulling forward inventory, reconfiguring supply chains, investing in compliance and origin planning, and delaying hard-to-reverse investment. Those defensive adjustments impose real costs even when threatened tariffs are never implemented or are withdrawn before meaningful revenue is collected. The Article uses President Trump's second term as a case study because it combines unusually frequent threats with aggressive testing of statutory and constitutional boundaries. It makes three contributions. First, it distinguishes shadow tariffs from ordinary incidence analysis and explains why reversal does not undo the harm. Second, it maps the private-law and operational channels through which volatility "collects" burdens. Third, it proposes a measurement strategy based on threat windows and observable proxies, and it shows why separation-of-powers design is economic policy in this setting.

title: When She Fails: Women Entrepreneurs and Gender Gaps in Business Bankruptcy
affiliations: Rutgers Business School - Rutgers University, University of Delaware, Rutgers Business School and Rutgers Business School at Newark and New Brunswick

detail.title: When She Fails: Women Entrepreneurs and Gender Gaps in Business Bankruptcy
detail.abstract: Female-owned firms are more likely to be pushed into liquidation and less likely to emerge successfully from bankruptcy than observably similar male-owned firms, and the gap widens sharply when courts are congested. In our data on U.S. small-business bankruptcies, female-owned firms are 24 percent more likely to file under Chapter 7 and, conditional on Chapter 11, are considerably less likely to receive a discharge. Evidence from 1.9 million SBA loan records shows little difference in observable pre-filing credit quality between female-and male-owned firms, weakening a simple creditworthiness explanation. This discharge penalty is concentrated among high-caseload judges. Eventstudy evidence around unexpected judicial departures, which raise surviving judges' workloads, shows the female gap widening after vacancy shocks. Women also respond on the filing margin, turning to Chapter 7 more often in congested courts, while experienced attorneys partly offset this avoidance without closing the discharge gap. The evidence points to a post-failure institutional friction in entrepreneurship.

detail.abstract:
The Efficiency Framework posits that reality consists of nested dissipative structures whose pri- mary function is the optimal channeling and dissipation of energy. The Golden Ratio (ϕ ≈ 1.618) emerges as the universal attractor for thermodynamic efficiency in open systems. By quantifying the ratio between Structural Integrity (En) and Entropy Production (Γ), this framework uni- fies subatomic decay, biological evolution, astrophysical processes, and macro-economic phase transitions under a single predictive calculus.

The Scaling Law of Resolution (τ ) demonstrates that time-to-resolution is a derivative of a system’s specific energy mass. The global instability observed in 2026 is a high-probability phase transition candidate governed by these constants.

title: The Micro-Dynamics of Algorithmic Discipline: A Mathematical Framework for Platform Labor
affiliations: Thammasat University

detail.title: The Micro-Dynamics of Algorithmic Discipline: A Mathematical Framework for Platform Labor
detail.abstract: This paper developsa self-contained mathematical framework for analyzing labor dynamics under algorithmic management in platform economies, with particular application to the food delivery gig economy. We formalize the micro-foundations of rider-agent behavior through a continuous three-dimensional state space integrating economic position, physiological condition, and psychological disposition, drawing on prospect theory, psychological contract theory, and occupational health science. The framework yields three core analytical results. Theorem 1 (Health Depletion Fixed Point) establishes existence, uniqueness, and local asymptotic stability of the health steady state under general convex damage and concave recovery functions. Theorem 2 (Endogenous Stratification) proves that income inequality, measured by the Gini coefficient, is monotonically increasing over time if and only if the platform's dispatch allocation function is strictly convex-formally identifying algorithmic convexity as the mathematical root of the Matthew Effect. Theorem 3 (Inverted-U Control) demonstrates the existence and uniqueness of an interior optimal control intensity that maximizes aggregate order fulfillment, arising from the tension between compliance gains and attrition losses. Together, these results provide a unified analytical foundation for agent-based simulation, empirical testing, and policy design in the platform labor literature.

detail.abstract:
Introduction: This study aimed to understand how Asian patients with non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) value different attributes of intravesical bladder treatments.

Methods: An online discrete choice experiment (DCE) was completed by NMIBC patients from Hong Kong, Singapore, South Korea, and Taiwan. Participants repeatedly chose between two hypothetical medical treatments (intravesical treatment and intravesical drug delivery device) that varied in seven attributes: frequency and duration of induction therapy; frequency of maintenance therapy; efficacy; risk of local side effects; risk of systemic side effects; aftercare required; and treatment cost. DCE preferences were analyzed using a mixed multinomial logit model. Relative attribute importance (RAI) scores were obtained to explore patients’ treatment priorities.

Results: The study included data from 92 NMIBC patients (68.5% male). Approximately two-thirds (66%) of respondents were aged between 40 and 59 years. All attributes, except out-of-pocket cost, significantly influenced patient treatment choice. The attributes ranked in order of importance to patients were: 1) risk of local side effects (RAI 27.14%); 2); aftercare required (RAI 24.19%); 3) risk of systemic side effects (RAI 19.52%); 4) efficacy (RAI 11.28%); 5) duration of induction therapy (RAI 9.89%); 6) frequency of maintenance therapy (RAI 6.48%); and 7) treatment cost (RAI 1.49%). There was a slightly higher predicted preference share for the intravesical treatment method (58.4%) than the intravesical drug delivery device (41.5%) when all attributes were kept equal, however the choice of holistic treatment approach was influenced by the treatment side effect profile and efficacy.

Conclusions: NMIBC Asian patients requiring intravesical cancer treatment prefer treatments that have the lowest side effect profile. Following side effects, patients value treatments that are effective in treating the cancer. Cost of treatment and mode of treatment delivery are not major influencing factors in treatment choice.

title: Measuring Dyadic Dynamics: A Hidden Markov Approach
affiliations: Southern Illinois University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Measuring Dyadic Dynamics: A Hidden Markov Approach
detail.abstract: People fall into destructive relational patterns without knowing they have done so, and they stay without knowing why. Clinicians who work with these patterns distinguish three dimensions, how much destructive interaction there is, what kind, and how fast it rotates, but no existing instrument returns separate numbers for each. This paper introduces a four-state Markov framework that does. Two boundary parameters identified from boundarycrossing transitions determine the total amount. Two internal parameters identified from within-drama transitions determine type and tempo. The separation is structural: boundary-setting therapy and restructuring therapy target different estimates, draw on different data, and can be tested independently using transition counts alone. A dual-LLM coding pipeline achieves substantial inter-rater reliability (κ = 0.623 four-state, κ = 0.731 binary) on motivational interviewing transcripts, comparable to trained human coders on established instruments. Low-quality sessions spend roughly a third of their time in destructive scripts; collaborative sessions show none. The same pipeline applied without modification to stranger conversations and task-disagreement dialogues returns near-zero drama in both: the framework finds what is there and does not find what is not. A hidden Markov model fitted to native clinical annotations recovers exactly four latent states by BIC; a second unrelated feature representation recovers the same number. Neither was built in; both emerged from the data. The stickiest recovered state persists at 91%, a clinically resonant number suggesting that productive interaction, like destructive interaction, is self-reinforcing once established. The automaticity runs in both directions.

title: Attention Allocation and Price Discovery
affiliations: Rutgers Business School - Rutgers University,  and University of Tulsa - Collins College of Business

detail.title: Attention Allocation and Price Discovery
detail.abstract: We study how the allocation of investor attention shapes price discovery. When the cost of accessing public information falls, investors may reallocate attention from firmspecific signals toward common, high-salience content. This reallocation can compress idiosyncratic volatility while slowing the incorporation of information into prices. We formalize this in a model of limited attention and short-side crowding. To test these predictions, we exploit the staggered rollout of mobile broadband (3G) across U.S. counties as exogenous shocks to information access. Local 3G entry worsens price discovery: cross-autocorrelation and PEAD rise, and idiosyncratic volatility falls. Search activity increases, confirming that attention shifts rather than expands. The deterioration is strongest in major financial centers, for meme-prone stocks, and among non-special names-and remains pronounced where institutional participation is greater. Lower idiosyncratic volatility need not signal a better information environment; broader access can erode price discovery when it homogenizes attention.

title: THE COLONIAL ROOTS OF CORRUPTION IN AFRICA: A Historical and Structural Analysis

detail.title: THE COLONIAL ROOTS OF CORRUPTION IN AFRICA: A Historical and Structural Analysis
detail.abstract: Contemporary corruption in Africa does not result from spontaneous emergence but is rooted in the continuity of a political and administrative order inherited from colonization. This article demonstrates that colonial powers established governance systems where public good capture was not a deviation but the normal functioning mode. Through comparative analysis of French, Belgian and British colonial models, the study reveals how each metropole developed specific mechanisms for extracting African resources while moralizing this predation through civilizing discourse. French centralization created "slush funds" systems; Belgian administration established brutal extraction; British "indirect rule" instrumentalized local chiefs as corruption relays. Far from being eradicated at independence, these structures were appropriated by postcolonial elites who perpetuated capture logics while adopting nationalist discourse. This historical analysis establishes that African corruption is not a cultural phenomenon but the product of colonial administrative engineering that deliberately organized public patrimony's availability for private capture. Understanding these roots is essential to conceiving structural solutions that break with this inherited order rather than merely moralizing individual behaviors.

title: Constitutionalizing Public Goods to Neutralize Corruption in Africa

detail.title: Constitutionalizing Public Goods to Neutralize Corruption in Africa
detail.abstract: Faced with the failure of behavioral approaches to fighting corruption in Africa, this article proposes a radical institutional innovation: the Patrimonial Shield Against Corruption. This mechanism is based on a simple but revolutionary conviction: it is more effective to neutralize the material effects of corruption than to indefinitely pursue its perpetrators. The article presents the complete architecture of this structural mechanism that articulates two inseparable pillars: (1) the constitutionalization of public goods conferring upon them a supreme legal status of inalienability, traceability and transparency; (2) the creation of a National Register of Patrimonial Assets ensuring permanent oversight of the collective patrimony. By reversing the burden of proof-all enrichment must be justified or face neutralization and reintegration into the public domain-the Shield transforms the relationship between the State, collective patrimony and citizen responsibility. This sovereignty engineering aims not to eradicate corruption through virtue, but to make its materialization impossible through structural coherence, thus substituting the logic of patrimonial coherence for that of aleatory trust.

detail.abstract: Background. The Government of Kenya plans to scale-up an adolescent-focused cash 'plus' programme to improve educational attainment and delay adolescent pregnancy. This study aimed to estimate the programme's impacts, economic returns, and cost-effectiveness using model-based economic evaluation. Methods. We modelled the delivery of conditional cash transfers 'plus' adolescent clubs, community conversations, parenting support and psychosocial support to poor adolescents in nine selected counties from 2026 to 2029. To estimate the programme's impact and economic returns, we compared two scenarios: a baseline in which intervention variables were held constant at 2025 levels, and an immediate scale-up sustained through 2026-2029. Human development impacts were simulated using an integrated model-based economic evaluation framework. Gains in years of schooling were projected with an education-transition model, while reductions in adolescent pregnancy, child marriage, and experiences of violence were estimated with a deterministic age-cohort transition model. Economic returns to schooling were calculated with Mincerian earnings functions. Model parameters were derived from rigorous impact evaluations, nationally representative surveys, and Kenya's national social registry. Cost-effectiveness ratios were benchmarked against published estimates from other adolescent-focused interventions. Findings. The four-year intervention, with an implementation cost of US$46.1 million, is projected to reach 140,000 adolescents. Compared to a baseline scenario, the intervention is estimated to yield an additional 74,900 (+7%) years of schooling; and avert 1,420 (-8%) adolescent pregnancies, 1,500 (-11%) child marriages, 2,970 (-3%) experiences of sexual violence, and 21,800 (-8%) experiences of emotional/physical violence. Furthermore, the intervention is projected to generate US$318 million in discounted gains in labour earnings, representing a seven-fold return on investment. The cost-effectiveness analysis estimates a cost of US$567 per additional year of schooling, and US$109 after discounting for programme impacts across multiple outcomes. Both figures are more favourable than published cost-effectiveness ratios for a merit scholarship intervention and a school uniform intervention. Findings were robust to sensitivity analyses, with a >98% probability that returns exceeded programme costs. Conclusion. An adolescent focused cash 'plus' programme is projected to improve adolescent human development, yielding substantial economic returns and favourable cost-effectiveness. Investments by governments and development partners in this area are likely to lead to safer, healthier, and more empowered lives.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the health consequences of hazardous pesticide exposure during a major regulatory phase-out that began in Turkey in the late 2000s. I combine individual birth histories from the Turkey Demographic and Health Surveys with newly constructed province-level measures of pesticide exposure. Exploiting geographic variation in pesticide use and the removal of hazardous active ingredients, I show that reductions in hazardous pesticides are associated with improved infant survival. The effects are concentrated among rural households and are primarily driven by male births. I find no comparable relationship for pesticides whose active ingredients were not banned, indicating that the effects reflect the toxicity of the banned compounds. I also find little evidence that the decline in hazardous pesticides affected agricultural production. Stronger effects in high-runoff provinces point to environmental exposure through water contamination.

title: Africa’s Third Independence: From the Proprietor-State to the Guardian-State

detail.title: Africa’s Third Independence: From the Proprietor-State to the Guardian-State
detail.abstract: Post-colonial African history has unfolded in two phases of emancipation: the first independence (1960s) conquered formal political sovereignty; the second independence attempted economic emancipation but encountered financial and technological dependence. This article conceptualizes Africa's Third Independence as the advent of patrimonial sovereignty-a nation's capacity to master, protect and valorize its common good. This transformation rests on a fundamental mutation: the transition from the proprietor-State (which holds and distributes resources according to allegiance logic) to the guardian-State (which protects the collective patrimony of which it is depositary, not owner). The article analyzes how the Patrimonial Revolution operates a decisive inversion by substituting the verticality of power with that of responsibility. State legitimacy is no longer measured by its capacity to impose, but by its capacity to account, preserve and transmit. This refoundation is accompanied by the emergence of a new patrimonial citizenship where citizens transition from passive administered status to active co-guardian of the common good. The resulting strategic State transforms development into a protection mechanism and returns to public action its primary meaning: transforming common resources into shared wealth and the common good into a foundation of sustainable sovereignty.

detail.abstract: I construct a Factor Uncertainty Index (FUI), inspired by Jurado, Ludvigson, and Ng (2015), measuring time-varying conditional volatility of forecast errors across 13 equity factor themes from Jensen et al. (2023). The FUI predicts future average factor theme returns with in-sample R² of 19-23% at h = 6 months and 22-30% at h = 12 months, confirmed out of sample by the Clark and West (2007) test, and predicts cross-sectional factor return dispersion with R² up to 52%. Predictability is concentrated in value/fundamental factor themes while risk/defensive and momentum/technical factor themes show no statistical response, consistent with time-varying compensation for fundamental valuation risk rather than limits-to-arbitrage frictions. Subperiod analysis reveals that predictability is episodic rather than uniform: it is strongest during periods of elevated cross-sectional factor uncertainty, especially during the dot-com era and the COVID-19 shock. The FUI dominates VIX, Jurado, Ludvigson, and Ng (2015) macro uncertainty, and Baker-Bloom-Davis (2016) policy uncertainty in horse race regressions; VIX enters with a negative and highly significant coefficient once factor-specific volatility is controlled for, suggesting that the two measures capture opposing economic channels. A volatility-managed portfolio scaling inversely with the FUI generates a spanning alpha of 7.33 basis points per month (t = 5.2), improving the annualized Sharpe ratio from 1.25 to 1.53.

title: THE FAILURE OF ANTI-CORRUPTION EFFORTS IN AFRICA: Diagnosis of a Methodological Impasse

detail.title: THE FAILURE OF ANTI-CORRUPTION EFFORTS IN AFRICA: Diagnosis of a Methodological Impasse
detail.abstract: Despite more than two decades of anti-corruption strategies supported by the international community, Africa remains the continent where corruption costs the most: 148 billion dollars per year according to the African Development Bank, representing 25% of continental GDP. This article examines the paradoxical failure of anticorruption policies in Africa and identifies the causes of a major methodological impasse. The analysis reveals that despite the multiplication of international conventions, specialized national agencies and legislative reforms, the gap between implemented mechanisms and obtained results continues to widen. The article documents the multiple dimensions of this failure: continuous aggravation of economic, financial and environmental costs; selective justice and elite impunity; ineffectiveness of "ghost agencies" created to satisfy international donors; perverse effects of perception indicators; and excessive bureaucratization of the international fighting system. The study demonstrates that the dominant behavioralist approachwhich aims to moralize individuals without securing structures-is fundamentally unsuited to the systemic nature of African corruption. This methodological impasse requires a paradigmatic break from an ethical logic to a structural logic of patrimonial flow neutralization.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This paper investigates the semi-strong form of market efficiency in the NIFTY 50 during the post-LLM era (2024-2025). Utilizing a corpus of over 73,000 headlines, the research employs a joint VAR(p)-GARCH(1,1) framework to test the 'Alpha Decay through Democratisation' hypothesis. We provide out-of-sample evidence that FinBERT-based sentiment signals no longer generate exploitable returns after accounting for India-specific transaction costs, while simultaneously documenting significant volatility clustering during the June 2024 Indian elections and 2025 US tariff announcements. Given the focus on behavioral finance, market microstructure, and financial econometrics in an emerging market context, we believe this is highly suitable for the Behavioral & Experimental Finance, Econometric Modeling, and Emerging Markets Finance eJournals.

detail.abstract: This paper tests whether transformer-based natural language processing (NLP) signals generate exploitable alpha in the NIFTY 50-India's benchmark equity index-using a real, two-year corpus of 73,118 financial news headlines from 600+ media outlets spanning January 2024 to December 2025. We construct a daily Composite Sentiment Index (CSI) using FinBERT (Huang et al., 2023) with a strict t-1 look-ahead-bias correction, and subject it to a joint VAR(p)-GARCH(1,1) econometric framework. Our central finding is a rejection of the predictive hypothesis: Granger causality from lagged sentiment to NIFTY 50 returns is statistically nonsignificant (F = 0.98, p = 0.43), and a sentiment-conditioned trading strategy underperforms the passive benchmark by 12.38 percentage points after India-specific transaction costs (STT 0.10%, market impact 0.05%, 18% GST on brokerage). However, the GARCH conditional volatility model reveals a different story: ARCH (α = 0.251 * * *) and GARCH (β = 0.392 * * *) effects are highly significant, and our data capture two major political shock events-the Indian general election of June 2024 (-6.1% single-day return, 325% conditional volatility spike) and the Trump tariff announcements of March-April 2025 (200% volatility spikes)-precisely where the GARCH model, but not the Granger test, responds.

title: Financial Coherence Catastrophes in Predicting Market Crashes

detail.title: Financial Coherence Catastrophes in Predicting Market Crashes
detail.abstract: Financial markets exhibit a troubling pattern: extended periods of apparent stability punctuated by sudden, catastrophic crashes that defy prediction by conventional models. This paper adapts the Experiential Coherence Framework (ECF) to financial markets, treating market crashes as coherence catastrophes-phase transitions where multiple dimensions of market functioning simultaneously break down. We develop a multi-dimensional framework that integrates narrative-data divergence, liquidity fragmentation, correlation breakdown, volatility regime instability, and institutional confidence into composite stress indices. Unlike traditional volatility models that are backward-looking and single-dimensional, our framework is forward-looking and captures the coupled dynamics of structural, behavioral, and informational factors. We validate the framework through historical analysis of three major crises (2008 Financial Crisis, 2010 Flash Crash, 2020 COVID Crash), agent-based simulations demonstrating market behavior under coherence stress, and Monte Carlo analysis of the coherence dynamics model. Results show that our Market Coherence Stress Index (MCSI) and Fragmentation Risk Index (FRI) provide early warning signals 30-60 days before peak crisis events, with critical thresholds (MCSI > 3.5, FRI > 0.5, coherence C < 0.3) identifying high crash risk. The framework offers superior predictive power compared to traditional approaches by capturing the rate of misalignment between market expectations and reality rather than merely measuring static levels of stress.

title: Safe-Haven Flows into the German Bond Market and the Role of Policy Disagreement
affiliations: University of Giessen, University of Giessen, University of Giessen - Department of Economics and Bank of Korea

detail.title: Safe-Haven Flows into the German Bond Market and the Role of Policy Disagreement
detail.abstract: German government debt is considered a safe asset in times of turbulence. We estimate the impact of changes in the risk appetite of global investors on weekly investment fund flows into the German sovereign bond market. Our key contribution is to allow the impact of such shocks to depend on the extent of disagreement about the path of fiscal policy, which we measure from the texts of all speeches delivered in the German Bundestag. An increase in global risk causes strong inflows into German government bonds if the coalition government is united, but only small and short-lived inflows if disagreement within the government is high. In contrast, disagreement between the government and the opposition has no moderating effect on fund inflows. We also find that the dependence of safe-haven flows on the prevailing level of fiscal disagreement is higher for actively managed funds and for funds domiciled abroad.

title: Who is afraid of Acting in Concert? The Platform Dilemma of Collaborative Shareholder Engagement

detail.title: Who is afraid of Acting in Concert? The Platform Dilemma of Collaborative Shareholder Engagement

This study was neither commissioned, funded, nor consulted by any of these companies. It is part of his PhD thesis.
