detail.abstract: On 28 February 2026, the United States and Israel launched a coordinated military assault on Iran while nuclear negotiations were actively underway. Now on its 28th day, the conflict has killed over 2,000 people including 1,407+ confirmed civilians and 210+ children, damaged 300+ health facilities, and triggered what the IEA describes as the greatest global energy security challenge in history. This paper argues that the US-Israel war on Iran is illegal under international law, constitutes an act of aggression under the UN Charter, and represents a catastrophic failure of the international rules-based order. Drawing on verified reporting from HRANA, Human Rights Watch, OHCHR, Al Jazeera, and the Washington Post, the paper examines the deliberate targeting of civilian infrastructure including the Minab girls school massacre, the assassination of state officials during active negotiations, the strategic implications of Iran's asymmetric response and Strait of Hormuz closure, and the global economic and diplomatic consequences of the conflict.

title: Synthetic, But How Much Risk Transfer?
affiliations: University of Zurich - Department Finance and

detail.title: Synthetic, But How Much Risk Transfer?
detail.abstract: Banks use synthetic risk transfers (SRTs) to offload potential losses in their loan portfolios to non-bank investors while retaining the loans on their balance sheets. We investigate this trillion-euro market using transaction-level data from the euro area, the largest SRT market, and highlight three channels of potential risks to financial stability. First, we show that banks synthetically transfer loans that are capital-expensive relative to their riskiness. To establish causality, we exploit a regulation that causes a jump in the risk weights of loans without affecting their riskiness. As banks redeploy the freed capital, their loan portfolios become riskier relative to their capitalization. Second, after entering an SRT, banks reduce their monitoring efforts compared to other banks lending to the same firm. The reduction in monitoring is greater the larger the share of their firm exposure that banks synthetically transfer. Third, banks and non-bank investors are interconnected. Banks are more likely to sell SRTs to investors with whom they already have credit relationship.

title: Asymmetric Resilience and the Transition to Multipolar Security Architecture: Focus on CBDC Interoperability for BRICS 2026

detail.abstract: The 2026 geopolitical environment marks a critical inflection point in global power dynamics. Traditional frameworks of conventional military and financial superiority are being offset by asymmetric leverage — decentralised, technology-enabled, and multi-stakeholder in nature. This memorandum presents a strategic roadmap for Regional Resilience and Financial Sovereignty across BRICS+ member states, grounded in three interlocking pillars: the doctrine of Technological Asymmetry in defence architecture; the transition to Currency Sovereignty through CBDC interoperability; and the 2026 geopolitical realignment of Gulf and Eastern Bloc financial relationships. The paper proposes the establishment of a BRICS Digital Currency Bridge (mBridge expansion) linking the e-Rupee, Digital Yuan, and Gulf-state CBDCs as a sovereign settlement ecosystem, bypassing USD-denominated infrastructure. It argues that India's BRICS 2026 Chairmanship represents a decisive window to formalise a Multipolar Financial Order.

title: Beyond Taxes: Should Automation be Regulated?
affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics, Zhejiang University - College of Economics, Peking University and Zhongnan University of Economics and Law - School of Economics

detail.title: Beyond Taxes: Should Automation be Regulated?
detail.abstract: Within a task-to-talent-and-robot assignment framework, this paper jointly designs automation regulation, robot taxation, and income taxation. In general, regulation and robot taxes that address displacement and productivity effects, respectively, are both desirable. However, in the absence of ability-complexity complementarity, regulation becomes undesirable, whereas robot taxation remains useful at compressing firms' rents. A quantitative analysis for the U.S. reveals: (i) optimal regulation targets low-income sectors; (ii) robot taxes are positive for high-income sectors and negative for low-income sectors, contrary to the no-regulation case; (iii) the policy package raises aggregate output by 4.81% and yields a welfare gain of 0.87%, with regulation accounting for more than 40% of both gains.

title: The Role of Digital Financial Literacy in Facilitating Climate-Smart Agriculture Adoption and Enhancing Food Security: Evidence from a Repeat Cross Sectional Household Survey in Cambodia

detail.title: The Role of Digital Financial Literacy in Facilitating Climate-Smart Agriculture Adoption and Enhancing Food Security: Evidence from a Repeat Cross Sectional Household Survey in Cambodia

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There is no conflict of interest in this study

The contents and research findings are solely the responsibility of the authors and do not necessarily represent the views of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT), Australia Award Cambodia (AAC), and Tetra International.

detail.abstract: Digital financial literacy (DFL) and climate-smart agriculture (CSA) are increasingly viewed as complementary levers for strengthening smallholder resilience and food security under rising climate risks, yet evidence on how digital capability translates into CSA adoption and improved food security remains limited, particularly in rural Cambodia where digitalization is expanding but households' ability to convert digital capability into climate adaptation remains uncertain. While the literature suggests that digital financial literacy and digital finance can relax constraints to CSA adoption-credit, information, and risk-management-evidence on the full pathway linking digital financial capability to CSA adoption and food security, especially in Cambodia and using mediated/structural models, remains limited, leaving policy design overly focused on platform expansion without sufficient attention to complementary enabling conditions. This paper examines whether and how digital financial literacy affects CSA adoption and subsequently improves food security among rural farming households in Cambodia. Using repeat cross-sectional household survey data collected in 2023 and 2025 across four provinces, we estimate determinants of DFS use and CSA adoption using logistic models with province and year fixed effects, assess joint adoption decisions across multiple CSA practices using a multivariate probit framework, and quantify direct and indirect (mediated) relationships between digital finance, CSA adoption, and household food security using a generalized structural equation model (GSEM) with ordered and binary HFIAS outcomes. Empirical results indicate that information/training exposure, perceived climate impacts, and social support are consistently associated with higher CSA adoption, while determinants of DFS use reflect a "capability and connectedness" pattern. In the structural models, CSA adoption is associated with a reduction of food insecurity, suggesting that CSA strongly protect households from the most acute food deprivation even when short-run adjustment costs persist. The findings underscore the need for integrated strategies that combine targeted digital financial capability building with strengthened extension and peerlearning systems and complementary rural infrastructure and market access to translate digital inclusion into wider CSA uptake and durable food security gains.

title: Transparency, Heterogeneity, and Public Information Design in Coordination Games

detail.title: Transparency, Heterogeneity, and Public Information Design in Coordination Games

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no relevant financial or non-financial interests to disclose.
declarations.funderStatement: Keiichi Morimoto is supported by JSPS KAKENHI Grant Nos. JP24K04895 and JP23K25535.

detail.abstract: Public information in coordination games does not merely change average welfare. With ex ante heterogeneity, it redistributes welfare across agents and creates winners and losers. I study a linear-quadratic Gaussian coordination game in which agents differ in private-signal precision and strategic interaction. The analysis yields a unique linear equilibrium, closedform type-level utilities, and a decomposition of the marginal effect of transparency into a precision channel and a composition channel. Under general heterogeneity, the composition channel factorizes into an agent-level exposure term and one aggregate coefficient, which delivers a tractable characterization of winner-loser incidence, a high-transparency Pareto region, and explicit low-transparency loser thresholds. I then introduce publicity as a separate design margin. Utilitarian dissemination concentrates coverage on poorly informed agents, whereas protected rules keep publicity broader to limit exclusion losses for strategically complementary agents. The results turn transparency into a distributional public information design problem.

title: Information in Prices
affiliations: University of Utah - David Eccles School of Business and KU Leuven, Department Accounting, Finance and Insurance

detail.title: Information in Prices
detail.abstract: Theory suggests that informational frictions lead to mispricing and resource misallocation. We empirically test how an exogenous upgrade to the public quote signal impacts price informativeness. We exploit the SEC's Rule 600(b) amendment that made round-lot size price-contingent, rendering some previously odd-lot quotes NBBO-eligible. Using an event-study design with synthetic difference-indifferences, we find that the improvement in the quote signal increases price informativeness and reduces noise in the price. Our results show how even minor enhancements in information dissemination can lead to meaningful improvements in market quality.

title: Euler Equalities Near Ruin
affiliations: Southern Illinois University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Euler Equalities Near Ruin
detail.abstract: The Euler equality is the most widely used condition in consumption economics, and it is valid on a subset of the state space. Near ruin, it stops being the right first-order condition. When ruin is irreversible and insurance is insufficient, the first-order conditions split into equalities far from ruin and inequalities near it. The gap is the value of survival. Far from ruin, the textbook holds, and a household satisfies orthogonality, adjusts buffers and consumption proportionally, with insurance remaining flat. Near ruin, the same household violates orthogonality, moves buffers before consumption, and shifts demand toward front-loaded payouts. Four decades of Euler puzzles spawned separate literatures, each with its own explanation. A common domain error runs through them: the equality was applied where only the inequality holds.

title: The Consumer City Revisited: Consumption Responses to Real-Time Population Presence
affiliations: Télécom Paris, Institut Polytechnique de Paris, McGill University - Department of Economics and Université Gustave Eiffel

detail.title: The Consumer City Revisited: Consumption Responses to Real-Time Population Presence
detail.abstract: This paper combines high-frequency mobile phone location data with card transaction records, to examine the relationship between the number of individuals present in a zone ('real-time population') and economic transactions. Using data from the metropolitan area of Lyon, France's second-largest urban area, and a Poisson Pseudo-Maximum Likelihood estimator, we estimate the elasticity of transactions with respect to a real-time count of individuals present in each of over one thousand zones. We document three key findings: (1) consumption responsiveness varies systematically across time and space, with elasticities peaking at 1.08 on Saturday midday but declining to 0.98 on Sunday and ranging from 1.04 in urban cores to 0.84 in peripheries; (2) spatial frictions reduce transaction flows by 2% per 1% increase in distance from home; and (3) sectoral heterogeneity, where essential goods (e.g., food retail) consistently outperform discretionary sectors (e.g., arts and entertainment). Together, these results underscore how temporal, spatial, and sectoral factors jointly shape economic activity.

title: The Borderline Constitution
affiliations: University of Colorado at Boulder - University of Colorado Law School

detail.title: The Borderline Constitution

publicationDetails.detailsText: U of Colorado Law Legal Studies Research Paper No. 26-13
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Colorado Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This Feature identifies and theorizes a distinct constitutional regime that federal courts have constructed at, adjacent to, and because of, the nation’s border. Drawing together strands of First, Fourth, Fifth, and Fourteenth Amendment law, along with habeas doctrine, constitutional torts, tribal sovereignty, and separation-of-powers concerns, this Feature demonstrates how constitutional guarantees systematically recede in the border’s shadow. These deviations from canonical and mainstream constitutional norms authorize intrusive state invasion of privacy and other fundamental rights, abdicate judicial oversight in favor of outsized executive discretion, and entrench racial and religious subordination.

 

The Feature further demonstrates that the effects of border exceptionalism do not remain geographically limited. Instead, the logic and tools of border exceptionalism increasingly migrate inward, shaping core doctrines in settings far outside formal border zones and impacting the lives of citizens and lawfully present noncitizens. This jurispathic diffusion can be traced through racial profiling of and diminished membership rights for Latine citizens; contracted habeas and due process protections; the erosion of constitutional tort remedies; and the normalization of militarized policing in mainstream doctrines with effects everywhere in the country. The result is a doctrinal migration capable of destabilizing our constitutional order writ large.

 

Finally, this Feature situates the borderline Constitution within the broader arc of constitutional development, identifying its affinities with anticanonical cases such as Korematsu v. United States, particularly in its reliance on militarized necessity and its willingness to subordinate equality to security. Unless repudiated or decisively constrained, the borderline Constitution threatens to transform locational exceptionalism into the rule. This Feature thus concludes by providing federal courts with a roadmap for paring back border exceptionalism, consonant with the reach and rationale of other bespoke constitutional locations.

title: Recursive Distributional Programming
affiliations: Southern Illinois University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Recursive Distributional Programming
detail.abstract: Dynamic equilibrium models routinely treat the mean of the distribution as a sufficient state variable. This paper shows that sufficiency holds under a precise condition the literature has not previously stated, and fails exactly where it matters most. It characterizes solutions to a Bellman equation defined over the space of wealth distributions and derives a single condition that answers when compression is valid. A low-dimensional summary retains all value-relevant information if and only if the marginal value of shifting wealth across the distribution can be expressed in terms of the statistics the summary retains. That condition organizes existing approaches from representative-agent to rich heterogeneous-agent models as different restrictions on a single object, and identifies the margin on which each fails. Near binding constraints, marginal value bends sharply and smooth projections cannot match the bend. The approximation error depends on two computable quantities: the severity of the bend and the mass the economy places near it. In quantitative experiments, a redistribution that leaves the mean unchanged alters subsequent capital dynamics and wages, and heterogeneous exposure to aggregate risk raises welfare costs by an order of magnitude over representative-agent benchmarks. The paper provides a diagnostic any model with a distributional state can evaluate: does the compressed state retain all value-relevant information, and if not, how much does the compression lose?

title: Belief Disagreement, Instability, and Uncertainty under Stochastic Recall
affiliations: University of Macau,  and National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER)

detail.title: Belief Disagreement, Instability, and Uncertainty under Stochastic Recall
detail.abstract: Using preregistered field studies, we show that even when individuals observe identical information, recall is highly heterogeneous across people and varies within the same person over time. Beliefs closely track recalled information and change even in the absence of new signals. Motivated by these findings, we develop a parsimonious model of stochastic recall in which agents store all observed signals but recall each past signal only probabilistically when forming beliefs, while updating optimally conditional on what they remember. This single friction generates cross-sectional disagreement, within-person belief instability, and heterogeneity in subjective uncertainty among ex ante identical individuals. The model yields sharp predictions for how disagreement, instability, and uncertainty vary with informational ambivalence, recall probability, and contextual cues. Large-scale preregistered experiments support these predictions, and survey evidence on macroeconomic and financial expectations is consistent with the model's implications. Our results identify stochastic recall as a foundational informational friction in expectation formation.

title: Turning a Blind Eye: Experimental Evidence on Strategic Non-monitoring
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Nanyang Technological University (NTU) - Division of Economics and Shanghai University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Turning a Blind Eye: Experimental Evidence on Strategic Non-monitoring
detail.abstract: Monitoring and punishment are commonly used to deter opportunistic behavior, and standard economic reasoning suggests that principals should acquire as much information as possible about agents' actions. Yet leaders often deliberately refrain from investigating potential misconduct. This paper studies such strategic non-monitoring in a laboratory experiment. A principal ("king") can costlessly investigate an agent's ("general's") action that benefits the agent at the principal's expense. Investigation reveals the action and triggers punishment but does not affect the principal's payoff. We find that many principals deliberately remain uninformed even when information is free. Leniency becomes more frequent when agents can reciprocate in a subsequent interaction, and agents reward principals who refrain from monitoring. These results suggest that avoiding information can function as a form of strategic leniency that helps sustain cooperation.

title: From Founders' Knowledge to Economic Value in Academic and Employee Startups
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison

detail.title: From Founders' Knowledge to Economic Value in Academic and Employee Startups
detail.abstract: Economic value capture is crucial for entrepreneurial startups, as it conditions the commercial viability of the technological opportunities underlying their founding. Startups vary in whether they capture value, and if so, whether through markets for product or technology. This study posits that value capture hinges on founders' knowledge accumulated in their prior employment context, separating founders as academic scientists and ex-employees of industry firms. Academic founders bring scientific knowledge from universities and employee founders carry industry-specific knowledge from their former employer. These differences provide the theoretical basis the study empirically explores in U.S. medical device startups. Academic startups tend to capture value in markets for technology, whereas employee startups tend to capture value in markets for product. Further, variations in founders' history and employment context can amplify or offset knowledge profiles within academic and employee startups toward scientific and commercial dimensions, shifting the resulting value capture pathway.

title: The Charge of Green Robots: From Environmental Robot Ethics to an Environmental Rule of Law for Robotics
affiliations: University of Turin - Faculty of Law, University of Turin, Department of Law,  and University of Turin

detail.title: The Charge of Green Robots: From Environmental Robot Ethics to an Environmental Rule of Law for Robotics
detail.abstract: Environmental robots-i.e. autonomous systems designed for ecological monitoring, conservation, and restoration-are increasingly crucial in addressing climate change and biodiversity loss. While offering benefits such as sustainable farming, waste reduction, and habitat protection, they also entail risks including resource use, ecological disruption, and accountability gaps. Current ethical frameworks and legal systems, particularly the EU's, partially address these challenges, often overlooking robots' environmental footprint and unintended harms. This paper argues for the integration of a new principle-the environmental rule of law-into robotics governance. Grounded in international and European legal traditions, this principle strengthens accountability and promotes eco-design as well as lifecycle responsibility by aligning robotics innovation with the human right to a clean, healthy, and sustainable environment. The analysis concludes that adopting the environmental rule of law is both necessary and feasible to ensure that robotics supports ecological sustainability rather than undermining it.

Korean Abstract: 
수도권 인구집중과 그 대응은 우리나라 최대 현안 중 하나이다. 본 연구는 수량적 공간일반균형모형을 활용하여 우리나라 도시규모분포의 결정요인을 구조적으로 추정하고, 지역정책의 효과와 현행 인구분포의 최적성을 정량적으로 분석함으로써 지역발전정책의 접근법과 가능성을 검토한다.

전국 161개 시군을 도시로 정의하고 2005~19년 자료를 분석한 결과, 동 기간 수도권 인구 비중 증가를 추동한 요인은 총요소생산성 격차였으며, 쾌적도와 인구수용비용 등 다른 요인은 이를 억제하는 방향으로 작동했다. 특히 2010년대에 발생한 거제, 구미, 울산 등 비수도권 제조업 도시의 총요소생산성 하락이 수도권 집중을 가속화했다. 2010년대 인구분산정책, 즉 혁신도시와 세종시 건설은 인프라 개선을 통해 해당 도시 인구를 일정 수준 성장시켰으나, 총요소생산성 개선이 부진하여 도시 성장 및 수도권 집중 완화 효과는 제한적이었다.

비수도권 7개 도시를 권역별 거점도시로 선정하여 육성하는 가상실험 결과, 수도권 비중을 2000년 수준으로 낮추기 위해서는 상당한 수준의 총요소생산성 및 인프라 효율성 개선이 필요하다. 이를 후생손실 없이 정당화할 수 있는 정책비용 상한 폭은 제한적이다. 이러한 투자로도 수도권 비중은 여전히 인구의 절반에 가깝다. 최적공간정책 분석 결과, 집적경제의 효율적 활용을 위해서는 전국 대도시로의 인구집중이 권고된다. 이때 서울뿐 아니라 부산 대구 광주 등 비수도권 대도시로도 인구가 재배치되어 수도권 집중은 2019년 수준에서 더 심화되지 않을 수 있다.

이 결과는 세 가지 시사점을 제공한다. 첫째, 수도권 집중의 핵심 요인은 생산성 변화로서, 지역발전정책이 실효성을 갖기 위해서는 생산성을 실질적으로 향상시키는 정책수단의 개발이 선행되어야 한다. 둘째, 낙관적 시나리오에서도 수도권 비중을 43% 이하로 낮추기 어려우며, 정책개입에는 선택과 집중이 요구된다. 셋째, 최적공간정책은 대도시 집중을 권고하나 이것이 반드시 수도권 집중 심화로 연결되지는 않는다. 수도권 집중 심화 방지가 목적이라면 권역별 거점도시 육성을 통한 선제적 공간구조 재편이 유효할 수 있다.

English Abstract: 
This study employs a quantitative spatial general equilibrium model to estimate the determinants of city size distribution in South Korea and quantify the effects of regional policies, evaluating the optimality of its current population distribution.

Defining 161 cities and counties nationwide as cities and analyzing data from 2005 to 2019, the study finds that differentials in total factor productivity (TFP) drove up the population share of the Seoul Metropolitan Area (SMA), while amenities and urban accommodation costs worked in the opposite direction. In particular, the TFP decline among non-SMA manufacturing cities, such as Geoje, Gumi, and Ulsan, during the 2010s accelerated concentration in the SMA. Although regional development initiatives in this period, including innovation cities and Sejong City, improved local infrastructure and supported moderate population growth, weak TFP gains limited their impact on alleviating SMA concentration.

These findings offer three policy implications. First, for regional development policies to be effective, they must include measures that boost regional productivity. Second, even under optimistic scenarios, reducing the SMA share below 40% remains challenging, suggesting that policy goals should be realistic and strategically focused. Third, to prevent further SMA concentration, proactive spatial restructuring through the development of regional hub cities could provide a path forward consistent with the Pareto optimum.

detail.abstract:
The right to use is a central element of property rights. But it is an under-analyzed aspect of the right to private property protected by the Takings Clause of the Fifth Amendment, which requires the government to pay “just compensation” whenever it takes “private property” for public use. Modern Supreme Court jurisprudence wrongly provides only modest protection for the right to use. This chapter makes the case for a strong right to use under the Takings Clause.

 Part I outlines the importance of the right to use property in the real world. For most types of property, that right is an essential element of the “bundle of sticks” possessed by the owner, often even the most important element. That point applies to both property in land, and personal property.  Part II makes the originalist case for a strong right to use under the Takings Clause. William Blackstone—a major influence on early American conceptions of property law and on the leading American Founders—regarded the right to use as a central element of property rights. The same was true of leading court decisions and legal theorists around the time when the Takings Clause and the rest of the Bill of Rights became “incorporated” against state and local governments in 1868.  Part II also gives a brief overview of the “police power” exception to Takings Clause liability and its relevance to the right to use. That exception would deny compensation in cases where the use restricted poses a significant threat to public health or safety. But it does not do so in other situations, including the vast majority of exclusionary zoning restrictions on housing construction.

detail.abstract: Cross-border electricity trade is key to grid decarbonization. However, trading often relies on bilateral Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs), imposing operational constraints that potentially compromise system-wide efficiency. Here, we quantify the opportunity costs that these long-term, static contracts pose for Mainland Southeast Asia, a region of 230 million people. Using a high-resolution, multi-sector modeling framework, we show that existing bilateral agreements impose an operating paradigm that is misaligned with the capability of physical assets. Relaxing PPA constraints could generate 3.2\% extra revenue to cover debt service of multiple hydropower projects, double the volume of regional energy exchange, and mitigate hydro-climate-induced price shocks. However, flexible trade yields unequal economic gains across participating countries and redistributes their carbon emissions by reducing hydropower curtailment, while simultaneously displacing expensive natural gas with coal. We show that PPAs are choke points, restricting electricity flow and partly driving the financial distress faced by regional state-owned enterprises.

detail.abstract: ntroducing payoff asymmetry in classical games has been shown to cause large inconsistencies between experimental behavior and theoretical predictions of the Nash Equilibrium, which cannot be explained with error and noise. In this paper, we propose the game geometric dispersion (G-GD) model which generalizes Nash as well as the widely studied linear models of other-regarding preferences in games. By introducing nonlinearity into the player's utility, G-GD allows the equilibrium to shift with changes in players' own payoffs. Drawing on extensive experimental evidence from the literature, we show that G-GD generates equilibrium outcomes more consistent with observed behavior than both Nash Equilibrium and prevailing otherregarding models, whether linear or non-linear. Unlike models with significant assumption of error and noise, G-GD retains simplicity and behavioral justifications. Using comparative empirical analysis of five game theory models, we demonstrate that G-GD offers a flexible, behaviorally grounded, and theoretically sound approach for understanding game theoretic strategic interactions, bridging the gap between theoretical predictions and experimental evidence. title: The Vanishing Economics of Trade Secret Value
affiliations: University of Nebraska at Lincoln - College of Law

detail.title: The Vanishing Economics of Trade Secret Value
detail.abstract:
Trade secret law is built around a simple economic fact. Information can yield supracompetitive returns only when prospective competitors are prevented from using it—as when it is kept secret from them. A successful trade secret plaintiff must therefore show that the alleged trade secret derives “independent economic value” from not being generally known to others. Yet modern doctrine sometimes treats this value requirement as something else—an inquiry into whether information is “valuable” in the abstract and whether it is independently useful versus dependent on some other information. Part of the reason is simply that proof of trade secret value is difficult. But another part lies in statutory drafting choices that have invited courts to take interpretive detours. Redundancy and indeterminacy in the statutory definitions encourage consideration of “value” as an abstract inquiry that can be proven by plaintiff-centric evidence, such as development costs or ongoing use, or defeated through categorical arguments about what type of information “counts.” The result is doctrine that recites the economic logic of trade secrecy while quietly drifting away from it.

The consequences are costly. When “value” loses its competitive referent, trade secret law becomes subject to misuse to protect business investments merely as such, invites unfruitful early motion practice, expands discovery, and turns trade secret remedies into competitive restraints untethered from their innovation- and competition-promoting function. This Article offers two modest corrections that make trade secrecy’s economic core harder to miss: first, it explains how the modifier “independent” functions in the statutory phrase “independent economic value”; second, it reframes the trade secret value requirement as an “economic advantage” requirement to place trade secrecy’s key definition in explicitly competitive terms. A trade secret is information that provides actual or potential economic advantage from not being generally known or readily ascertainable by proper means by competitors who could make use of it. With economic advantage as the measure, “value” means what it should—secrecy-derived rents from delayed market entry and imitation.

title: Same Language, Different Markets: Labor Market Competition between Mexican and Hispanic Immigrants in the United States

detail.title: Same Language, Different Markets: Labor Market Competition between Mexican and Hispanic Immigrants in the United States
detail.abstract: Within-skill and cross-skill competition among Hispanic immigrants operate through distinct mechanisms with opposite geographic patterns. Using Census data from 1980 to 2020 and shift-share instrumental variables following Card (2001, 2009), I find that within-skill competition among low-skilled workers is driven entirely by California, Texas, and Florida; excluding these states eliminates the effect. Cross-skill competition shows the opposite pattern: low-skilled Mexican and high-skilled Hispanic workers are imperfect substitutes nationally, but estimates are insignificant within these three states alone and strengthen when excluding them. This divergence indicates that network-based segmentation requires thick immigrant labor markets to sustain origin-specific hiring channels, while cross-skill substitution is most visible in thinner markets where occupational sorting is less developed. Cross-skill competition is asymmetric: low-skilled Mexican immigration widens wage gaps with high-skilled Hispanics, while the reverse effect is zero, consistent with downward skill transferability and credential barriers limiting upward substitution. Instrument diagnostics confirm that identification is not driven by any single origin country. The structure of immigrant labor market competition cannot be characterized by a single national elasticity; skill composition and geographic concentration jointly determine competitive outcomes.

title: The Inversion of Doubt: Public Skepticism Is Concentrated Where Epistemic Warrant Is Highest and Absent Where It Is Lowest

detail.title: The Inversion of Doubt: Public Skepticism Is Concentrated Where Epistemic Warrant Is Highest and Absent Where It Is Lowest
detail.abstract: Public skepticism is not randomly distributed across scientific domains. This paper argues that it is distributed inversely to where it is epistemically warranted: the scientific claims attracting the most sustained public doubt are among the most empirically robust in the history of inquiry, while claims with documented failure rates of 40 to 97 percent circulate with near-zero friction. This inversion is not the product of individual irrationality. It is structurally produced by three forces: the asymmetry between falsifiability timescales in hard versus soft science, identity-protective cognition that indexes skepticism to perceived threat rather than accuracy, and a selection environment that rewards transmissibility over calibration. The paper synthesizes evidence from Delphi foresight retrospectives, metascientific positive-result analyses, geopolitical forecasting tournaments, clinical reversal epidemiology, and longitudinal public opinion data to document both the inversion and its mechanisms. A secondary finding concerns the measurement infrastructure itself: the absence of dual-cohort survey data measuring public skepticism toward social science claims is not an oversight but a structural consequence of unfalsifiability. Where ground truth is unavailable, the correction machinery never activates, and claims circulate without measurement or challenge. The cross-domain synthesis offered here-arguing that high acceptance rate is evidence of low accuracy above a threshold-has not previously been formalized in the philosophy of science literature, though its component mechanisms have been documented in isolation across metascience, forecasting research, risk psychology, and science communication. A provisional threshold operationalization is offered, proposing that domains meeting two of three measurable criteria-registered report divergence exceeding 20 percentage points, expert calibration gap exceeding 20 percentage points, and falsifiability timescale exceeding a professional generation-warrant presumptive skepticism of public acceptance rates.

detail.title: Competitive Salaries and Enforcement Productivity: Evidence from Medicaid Fraud Control Units
detail.abstract: Does paying public employees more improve government performance? Private-sector research estimates pay-productivity elasticities of 0.04 to 0.10 (Wallskog et al., 2026), driven primarily by performance-based pay, but whether a comparable relationship exists in public agencies, where performance bonuses are rare, remains an open question. We examine this using state Medicaid Fraud Control Units (MFCUs), law enforcement agencies that investigate and prosecute healthcare provider fraud under civil service salary schedules with no performance pay. Using a panel of 52 jurisdictions over 2006-2024, we estimate two-way fixed effects models relating within-state variation in real salary (deflated by Bureau of Economic Analysis Regional Price Parities) to a composite enforcement index. Each $10,000 increase in real salary predicts a 0.031 standard deviation increase in enforcement output (p = 0.019, state-clustered standard errors). For a typical 39-person unit, this translates to approximately 2.2 additional enforcement actions per year, a 2.9 percent increase relative to the mean enforcement rate. The implied pay-productivity elasticity is 0.16 (p = 0.049, 95% CI [0.001, 0.316]). The point estimate is comparable to private-sector estimates where performance pay drives the relationship, though the wide confidence interval precludes precise comparison. Because MFCUs lack performance bonuses, the effect operates through a selection channel: competitive salaries attract and retain more productive investigators and prosecutors. The result survives all eight standard error specifications tested, leave-one-out analysis (51 of 52 states significant at p < 0.05), permutation inference (p < 0.001), falsification tests against placebo outcomes, and the addition of state-specific linear trends.

detail.abstract: AI tools designed to help legitimate users may simultaneously lower the cost of fabrication. detail.abstract: Intellectual property ("IP") has progressively become a tool of the United States' economic and trade diplomacy to a degree that isolates the United States from developing countries and sometimes its traditional allies, including Australia and New Zealand. title: The Political Economy of National Identity
affiliations: Hebrew University of Jerusalem - Political Science Department and The Hebrew University of Jerusalem - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Political Economy of National Identity
detail.abstract:
National identity is a powerful force in contemporary politics, but its effects vary across contexts. This chapter synthesizes research on how national identity shapes economic and political outcomes when it competes with other group identities. We employ a conceptual framework in which individuals weigh national identity against alternative identities such as economic class, ethnicity, partisanship, and supranational affiliations. The relative salience of these identities determines attitudes and behaviors across multiple domains. 
We review evidence across five main areas. In international trade, we examine how national identity affects consumer behavior, policy preferences, and trade wars. In redistribution politics, we review how competition between national and class identities shapes welfare preferences, and how ethnic diversity and immigration affect redistribution. In conflict settings, we analyze how national identification influences both civil war and ethnic violence within countries, and military conflict between nations. We examine how nationalist parties translate preferences into policy once in power, covering immigration, welfare chauvinism, family and fertility policies, and foreign affairs. Finally, we discuss whether shared national identity can reduce partisan polarization. 
Two general lessons emerge. First, national identity shapes political and economic outcomes far beyond populism, xenophobia, and immigration. Second, understanding the political-economy implications of national identity requires identifying the salient alternative identities with which it competes in each setting, and analyzing when it dominates in equilibrium. This helps assess when national identity is likely to support free trade or induce trade wars, increase or decrease support for redistribution, intensify or prevent conflict, unite or divide partisans.

detail.abstract: This study aims to determine the tax revenue loss due to unrealised capital gains in the United States between 2000 and 2025, filling a major information gap in the literature on tax evasion based on wealth. We outline four complementary policy options: a progressive mark-to-market tax, a deferred tax account, graduated accrual taxation, and an estate appreciation surtax that can raise $90-150 billion per year, while correcting the fundamental inequities in the tax treatment of labour and capital income.

This study assessed the Impact of T4K: TEKNIKAL NA KAALAMAN, KASANAYAN, KAGALINGAN PARA SA KABUHAYAN on the Alternative Learning System (ALS), Bambang I District, particularly to the learners of Alternative Learning System, Bambang District 1.

The project was implemented by the College of Industrial Technology at Nueva Vizcaya State University, Bambang Campus which commenced on 2022 which aimed at providing entrepreneurial skills to the identified beneficiaries. The implementation includes series of technical and skills training along the different fields of the BSIT Program, BSIMe and BSCS.

Mixed method of quantitative and qualitative research approach was utilized to assess the extent of the extension services to the socioeconomic status of the beneficiaries, its contribution to the organization and the challenges and its correlations to improve the services.

Frequency counts, percentages and correlation were used to treat data quantitatively while percentiles from the qualitative were transcribed verbatim. Results showed that the extension services resonate well with young adults who are often in the phase of building their careers and lives.

There were 17 ALS trainees under the ALS beneficiaries. The introduction of this project to the ALS was an avenue in increasing the income of beneficiaries from Php5,500.00 to at least reach the food threshold and poverty threshold of Php9,550.00 and Php13,797.00 respectively showing a significant relationship to their social life.

Despite encountering challenges and weaknesses such as limited time allocation and diverse participants, the extension services demonstrated skills development among participants. This research provides valuable insights for program improvement and emphasizes the importance of holistic approaches to community engagement and development.

The K-Shaped Economy 

Divergent Fortunes Across American Counties and the Potential Impact on the 2026 and 2028 Elections
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the K-shaped U.S. economy of 2025-2026, where high-income asset owners ascend while rural communities and lower-wage households decline. It documents structural drivers-wealth concentration, tariffs, wage divergence, interest rate policy, and AI displacement-and maps the geographic paradox whereby Trumpmajority counties (86% of all counties, 38% of GDP) depend disproportionately on federal programs their coalition seeks to reduce. The analysis assesses electoral implications for 2026-2028 and evaluates orthodox versus Modern Monetary Theory policy frameworks, finding that current fiscal architecture channels benefits upward while imposing costs on rural peripheries.

title: Are You Betting on Sustainability?
affiliations: University of Bologna - Department of Economics

detail.title: Are You Betting on Sustainability?
detail.abstract: When the sustainability of assets is priced, its impact on discount rates depends not only on the asset's sustainability but intrinsically also on its risk profile. This has implications often overlooked in portfolios used to assess the sustainability premium or to hedge sustainability-related shocks. Specifically, the average returns of sustainability-sorted long-short portfolios are shaped by the risk profiles of their components, even when the portfolio is risk-neutral, which also affects the portfolio's sensitivity to shifts in sustainability concerns. Using Refinitiv ESG scores for US stocks, a weak sustainability premium is observed, whose significance differs importantly from that of the plain long-short portfolio returns.

detail.title: Population Structure and Digital Financial Inclusion
detail.abstract: The aim of this article is to empirically examine the impact of population structure on digital financial inclusion after controlling for GDP per capita growth, inflation, unemployment, institutional governance quality and bank stability. The data are analysed for 216 countries from 2004 to 2023 using the two-stage system GMM regression methodology. The results find that digital financial inclusion is higher in urban and young populations and in countries with a rapid population growth rate. Digital financial inclusion is lower in vulnerable and non-vulnerable populations. Interaction analyses show that institutional quality increases digital financial inclusion in the rural population while high inflation constrains it. High unemployment worsens digital financial inclusion in the older population. Digital financial inclusion is higher among the vulnerable population during periods of high inflation. Strong institutional quality and a high unemployment rate lead to higher digital financial inclusion in the non-vulnerable population.

detail.abstract:
Building on the Institute’s foundational work on integrating AI into investment frameworks (2025), this report takes the perspective of an asset owner evaluating an asset manager across fixed income, public equity, private equity, and hedge funds. Three findings frame the analysis.

●      The disruption risk is real and accelerating. AI now ingests, synthesizes, and acts on information at speeds and scales that dwarf human capacity, and the competitive gap between early adopters and unprepared managers is already measurable.

●      The risk is not uniform. Liquid, data-rich markets face the most immediate disruption; private markets have a longer runway but are not immune.

●      AI readiness is now non-negotiable. Managers unable to articulate a credible AI strategy risk falling outside the investable universe for technologically sophisticated allocators.

In the analysis, the Institute of Sovereign Investors offers some guidance. Based on our experience, we propose tools to assist allocators in building AI-resilient teams of external managers.

detail.title: Brick by Brick: The Global North Exports Climate Breakdown to the Global South -A Case Study of Exploitation of Labour in the India-UK Brick Industry
detail.abstract: Climate colonialism reflects a structural imbalance wherein the Global North externalizes ecological and human costs to the Global South, perpetuating a cycle of dependence and exploitation. This paper investigates the phenomenon through the India-UK brick trade, revealing how Northern consumption patterns sustain environmental degradation and labour exploitation in Southern economies. Using a mixed-methods framework combining trade data, field interviews with 150 kiln workers in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, and environmental modeling of black carbon emissions, the study quantifies the extent of carbon and social inequity embedded in the brick supply chain. Findings show that over 400 million UK-imported bricks annually produce threefold higher carbon emissions compared to domestic production, contributing approximately 16 million tons of CO₂ to India's emissions each year. This offshored production excarbates climate vulnerability while reinforcing bonded labour systems that trap over 20 million migrant workers, 5 million of them children under hazardous exploitative condition with negligible pay. Through a telecoupling and decolonial political economy lens, the study connects UK demand to systemic outcomes including deforest station, soil degradation and public health burdens and it criticizes the inadequacies of voluntary frameworks like the UK Modern Slavery Act 2015 and highlights how greenwashed net zero narratives obscure neo-colonial dependencies. The analysis concludes that Global climate governance remains inequitable; developing Nation lack the financial and technological capacity to meet emission target while the Global North climate finance mandatory due diligence in supply chains and investment and clean technology to interest these are symmetry ultimate argues that dismantling climate colonialism requires rebuilding global policy frameworks to ensure justice based, equitable climate transitions; brick by brick.

title: Intraday Stochastic Drift
affiliations: University of Verona - Department of Economics and University of Verona

detail.title: Intraday Stochastic Drift
detail.abstract: We study drift dynamics in intraday financial returns using a semiparametric approach based on the conventional semimartingale representation of asset prices. Our framework allows us to formally test for the presence of stochastic drift dynamics in the data and to assess its impact on the daily return volatility. The main empirical results we find are the following: (i) there exists compelling evidence of intraday drift dynamics in stock returns; (ii) drift episodes are persistent over time and can be predicted based on past data, offering potential for real-time monitoring of market instability; (iii) this form of predictability cannot be used to generate out-of-sample profits in momentum strategies once transaction costs are taken into account; (iv) when the drift moves significantly, our method provides a better measure of volatility compared to traditional estimators neglecting the randomness of the drift process.

detail.abstract: Smallholder farmers play a critical role in agricultural production and rural livelihoods in developing countries, yet they often face persistent challenges such as limited access to quality inputs, credit, markets, and extension services. One Acre Fund is a prominent agricultural organization that provides integrated support to smallholder farmers, including financing for farm inputs, training on improved farming practices, and market facilitation. This study assesses the impact of One Acre Fund's interventions on the economic status of smallholder farmers. Using a mixed-methods research design, the study compares beneficiaries from before and after joining OAF households to evaluate changes in key economic indicators such as farm productivity, household income, asset ownership, savings, and reduction on reliance in handouts. Quantitative data are analyzed using descriptive techniques, while qualitative data from interviews and focus group discussions provide contextual insights into farmers' experiences. The findings are expected to reveal the extent to which participation in One Acre Fund programs contributes to improved agricultural yields, increased income stability, and enhanced overall economic well-being of smallholder farmers. The study aims to inform policymakers, development practitioners, and agricultural organizations on the effectiveness of integrated agricultural support programs and to provide evidence-based recommendations for scaling and improving interventions targeted at smallholder farmers.

detail.title: Financial Conditions Targeting in a Multi-Asset Open Economy
detail.abstract: We analyze monetary policy responses to noisy …nancial conditions in an open economy where exchange rates and domestic asset prices a¤ect aggregate demand. Noise traders operate in both markets, and specialized arbitrageurs have limited risk-bearing capacity. Monetary policy creates cross-market spillovers: by adjusting the interest rate to stabilize one market, the central bank in ‡uences volatility in the other. We show that targeting a …nancial conditions index (FCI)-a weighted average of exchange rates and domestic asset prices-delivers substantial macroeconomic bene…ts. FCI targeting commits the central bank to respond to unexpected movements in …nancial conditions beyond what discretionary monetary policy implies. These stronger responses improve diversi…cation across markets: each market becomes more exposed to external shocks but less exposed to its own. This reduces volatility in both markets and activates the recruitment e¤ect from Caballero et al. (2025b) in each market-lower variance induces arbitrageurs to trade against noise, further dampening volatility. Foreign exchange (FX) targeting can also be e¤ective when the exchange rate is the primary source of noise, with bene…ts that increase as the economy becomes more open. In this case, FX targeting recruits arbitrageurs to stabilize the FX market, reducing volatility and dampening the macroeconomic impact of noise. However, FX targeting also raises volatility in non-targeted markets through anti-recruitment e¤ects, limiting its e¤ectiveness relative to FCI targeting, especially when domestic asset markets also matter for …nancial conditions and are comparably noisy.

detail.title: Legal Constraints on Intelligence Activities in Armed Conflict and Occupation

publicationDetails.detailsText: LAW IN THE SHADOWS OF WAR: ESPIONAGE AND SABOTAGE IN MODERN CONFLICT, Watkin & West, eds., (University of Toronto Press, forthcoming 2026).
Indiana Legal Studies Research Paper No. 572

detail.abstract:
In the short period between the end of the Cold War and the Snowden revelations, the international law of intelligence underwent a striking reversal: it now speaks with greater precision and nuance in times of peace than it does in times of war. While peacetime surveillance is increasingly governed by an elaborate and evolving body of international human rights law (IHRL), wartime intelligence remains anchored to a far shallower, mid-twentieth-century foundation of international humanitarian law (IHL) that has scarcely advanced since its codification. This static regime is often misinterpreted as providing a boundless license to spy in war. However, as the chapter demonstrates, this permissiveness is frequently presented as more absolute than originally envisioned.

The regulatory inadequacies of the law of wartime intelligence are examined further through a close doctrinal analysis of the CIA’s 2011 vaccination ruse in Pakistan. The chapter highlights how existing doctrines and legal categories in IHL—including ruses of war, perfidy, misuse of protective emblems, and the duty of constant care—struggle to meaningfully constrain one of the most hazardous and low-odds intelligence ploys of recent decades. Rather than providing clear limits, these frameworks expose deep indeterminacies in the law: permissive baseline rules qualified by underdeveloped or contested prohibitions.

The inadequacy of these frameworks multiplies exponentially in the face of "surveillant assemblages”. These contemporary assemblages are networked systems of AI-enabled monitoring, mass data extraction, and predictive analytics that operate continuously and opaquely, transforming entire societies into living data fields. Especially visible in situations of prolonged occupation, these assemblages allow powers to transcend the principle of temporariness, fundamentally "corrupting the normative regime of occupation”. Surveillant assemblages destabilize the normative foundations of IHL by diffusing harm and enabling new forms of control that exceed the law’s traditional vocabulary. To address this impasse, this chapter proposes a reorientation: an international law of wartime intelligence conceived as a non-formalist "legal assemblage". By rejecting hyper-positivism and allowing a fluid transportation of norms across IHL, IHRL, data protection regimes, and other specialized frameworks, the law can finally mirror the complexity of the twenty-first-century architectures of control it seeks to regulate.

detail.abstract: Generative AI has broken the assumption that online assessment performance reflects student knowledge, and the traditional countermeasures-proctoring software, AI detectors, lockdown browsers-are expensive, adversarial, and increasingly ineffective. This paper proposes a different paradigm: random post-assessment audits with credible penalties, modeled on the sampling-based enforcement strategies used in tax auditing, financial regulation, anti-doping, and nuclear nonproliferation. A game-theoretic analysis shows that with a penalty of 200 points (on a 100 point assessment) and a two-audit appeal mechanism, an instructor needs to conduct only 2-4 brief conversations per assessment in a class of 30 to make cheating irrational. The false positive rate-not the audit rate-is the critical parameter that determines fairness to honest students, and a two-audit appeal reduces the effective false positive rate to levels where a modest point bonus makes honest high-performers net beneficiaries of the system. An accompanying interactive simulator allows instructors to calibrate parameters for their own courses. The paper concludes with a call for small-scale pilot studies to empirically validate the framework before broad adoption.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between firm intangible investment, leverage, and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance. Using an unbalanced panel of 1,824 publicly listed US firms from 2015 to 2023, we find a strong negative relationship between intangible investment and leverage, consistent with the debt overhang hypothesis. Importantly, our results show that strong ESG performance significantly mitigates the negative relationship between leverage and intangible investment. The moderating effect of ESG is particularly pronounced for investment in intangible rather than physical capital. We propose that ESG performance moderates investment constraints through three pillarspecific economic channels: the environmental risk channel, the social capital channel, and the agency channel. The moderating role is driven primarily by the environmental risk and agency channels, with environmental performance being critical for investment in knowledge capital and governance performance for investment in organisational capital. The buffering effect of ESG is strongest for highly leveraged firms, where financing constraints are most binding, and for high-growth firms with abundant investment opportunities.

detail.abstract: We estimate the liquidity elasticity beta, governing how quickly market-maker depth withdraws as volatility rises, across N = 1,543 instruments: 43 CME futures from tick microstructure and 1,500 US equities from 10 years of Polygon minute bars via Corwin-Schultz spreads. The estimated elasticities form a continuous spectrum from beta = +2.00 (leveraged ETFs) to -0.33 (Treasury-bill ETFs), with coherent sector differentiation: equity ETFs (+0.76) > energy (+0.73) > banks (+0.64) > tech (+0.52) > healthcare (+0.38); 98.0% of equities show positive beta (92.1% significant at 5%). Treasury-bill ETFs are the only sector with uniformly significant negative beta, the predicted safe-haven stabilizing regime. We interpret this spectrum through a capital-weighted Kuramoto phase oscillator model, where the coupling K(r) = K_0(1 + gamma r^{2 delta})^{(beta-1)/2} emerges endogenously from a microstructural feedback loop and beta partitions the dynamics into stabilizing, withdrawing, and destabilizing regimes. During the March 2020 COVID crash (1,312 instruments), the aggregate Kuramoto order parameter r(t) peaks at 0.14, far below the calibrated activation threshold (r > 0.85), confirming that the endogenous feedback remains latent even under extreme stress, while individual instruments transiently reach full synchronization (r = 1) where the feedback mechanism activates. Against a naive rolling correlation benchmark (N = 1,500), the Kuramoto r(t) significantly outperforms for drawdown prediction (paired t = 3.04, p = 0.002; win rate 55.8%) and captures orthogonal information (Spearman between measures: -0.007). Per-instrument cross-validation at N = 1,538 reveals regime-dependent dynamics: within equities (Spearman r_s = +0.061, p = 0.018), the relationship is weakly positive; the CME-only subset (N = 38) shows the predicted negative direction (Spearman r_s = -0.22, p = 0.19). The framework provides regime-conditioned tools for crowding detection and capacity estimation.

detail.abstract: The Pan-African Investment Code (PAIC), as the first African model investment treaty, has received harsh criticism from investment experts who have labelled the instrument as 'too protectionist'. African experts drafted the PAIC to promote sustainable development by including non-traditional and groundbreaking features that concern Africa, making the model treaty a unique legal instrument. Those who criticise the PAIC for its protectionist approach towards investment and investors' rights and responsibilities assert that the PAIC is incompatible with sustainable development. This chapter argues that the PAIC, as a nontraditional instrument, is a powerful guiding source that can be used to promote sustainable development within Africa and the rest of the world. The chapter further argues that the PAIC should be used to negotiate the investment protocol of the African Continental Free Trade Area' AfCFTA' because the PAIC embraces modern views that are tailored to the needs of Africa, and it stresses the need to promote sustainable development, state-police-power to regulate for health safety, and good governance of investment laws within the continent. The PAIC endorses the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), which makes the PAIC well-situated to be used to negotiate the investment protocol of the AfCFTA because it removes the asymmetrical relationship between intra-African and extra-African investors and host states in Africa.

detail.abstract: Spokeo v. Robins represented a potentially sweeping change to standing doctrine, but its lack of clarity  left its ultimate impact on the law uncertain.  Several studies have measured Twiqbal’s impact, but to our knowledge, Spokeo’s impact has received no empirical attention despite its potential to nullify statutory requirements. We fill this gap by examining filings from Ninth Circuit cases.  We employ a “straddle design” to control for filing selection, comparing a treatment sample exposed to Spokeo with a control sample. We find evidence of large defendant motion selection and early settlement selection.  While we find that 25 percent of cases dismissed under Spokeo would have been negatively affected compared to the counterfactual, we find mixed evidence that Spokeo actually changed the legal standard.  The impact of Spokeo (both selection and judicial treatment) is confined to class actions, with any judicial treatment effects primarily concentrated on TCPA cases.

title: Games and Social Choice
affiliations: and University of Strasbourg

detail.title: Games and Social Choice
detail.abstract: This article reexamines the contexts in which Arrow's Social Choice and Individual Values (1951) emerged, clarifying the often acknowledged yet unexplained influence of Theory of Games and Economic Behavior. It situates Arrow's work within his training in logic and statistics in 1940s New York and the postwar cross-disciplinary environments of the Cowles Commission and the RAND Corporation, where economists, mathematicians, statisticians, and logicians redefined rational decision-making and aggregation. Completing his dissertation, Arrow occupied a distinctive position at the intersection of new research programs. At RAND, he worked on statistical decision theory and game theory alongside researchers extending game theory to diverse projects, while developing "The Possibility of a Universal Welfare Function" (1948), an early statement of social choice theory. Tracing the path from The Possibility to Social Choice, the article shows how Arrow adapted the mathematics of order sets from Theory of Games while rejecting its strategic and utilitarian conception of economic and political life. This framework shaped the problems, tools, and paradoxes informing his impossibility result. Recast within welfare economics, it integrated value judgments and echoed von Neumann and Morgenstern's concerns about the relation between individual and collective choice in their theory of cooperative games beyond formal rules.

title: The Geoeconomics of Trade in Critical Raw Materials
affiliations: Florida International University (FIU) - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Geoeconomics of Trade in Critical Raw Materials
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the extent to which free trade agreements mitigate the adverse commercial effects of geopolitical friction in critical raw material markets. Using a multi-product structural gravity model augmented with an interaction term, we analyze a comprehensive panel dataset of annual bilateral trade data covering 30 distinct critical raw materials across 233 countries from 1995 to 2021. Our empirical estimations rely on the Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood estimator and reveal that these commodities fundamentally deviate from standard trade expectations. First, highly concentrated critical raw materials initially exhibit strategic stockpiling, where diplomatic friction increases bilateral trade volumes. Second, while formal trade agreements act as an institutional shield against this volatility, their effectiveness is strictly conditional on market structure. For materials reliant on long-term contracts, strategic dependency is a chronic feature, and trade agreements provide durable protection across consecutive years. Conversely, for materials lacking long-term contracting structures, the initial stockpiling is a temporary response that reverses into significant trade reductions within a one-year lag, rendering formal trade agreements statistically ineffective. By systematically quantifying this temporal resilience channel, our study demonstrates that while trade agreements are important instruments for geoeconomic security, they are structurally insufficient for the most concentrated ores, highlighting the need for alternative sovereignty strategies such as domestic recycling and innovation.

detail.abstract: Generating novel ideas is fundamental to the design process; it requires deep expertise and contextual knowledge to do well. Yet, that same expertise and context can create barriers to generating innovation, locking solvers into traditional solving approaches. One way to overcome this tension is to open problems to outsiders – solvers from other domains who can attach their domain’s solving heuristics to your problem. While the growing adoption of open and distributed innovation has seen successful, a systematic way to attract surprise outsiders remains elusive. This paper offers a set of “context work” practices as a way to bridge disciplinary divides in cross-boundary problem solving. Leveraging a decades long sequence of field studies at NASA, this paper 1) induces three key dimensions of “context work,” 2) integrates them to define four alternative formulations for a given problem and 3) tests the impact of formulation on who is attracted to solve, and the quality of their solutions. We find a tension between attracting a greater number of new solvers with different expertise and receiving high quality solutions from them. We conclude by relating these findings to emerging opportunities to improve the adoption of generative AI in the design process.

title: The Equity Premium Puzzle, Solved: Monetary Debasement, Inflation Incentives, and the Structural Transfer from Lenders to Owners
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and Independent

detail.title: The Equity Premium Puzzle, Solved: Monetary Debasement, Inflation Incentives, and the Structural Transfer from Lenders to Owners
detail.abstract: The equity premium puzzle - the phenomenon that equities have outperformed risk-free government debt by 6-8% annually for over a century, far exceeding what standard models can explain with reasonable risk aversion - has been called the biggest unsolved problem in academic finance.  This paper argues the puzzle is solvable, and that its persistence reflects a misclassification: it has been treated as an asset pricing problem when it is fundamentally a political economy problem.  We identify three distinct layers composing the observed premium.  First, a genuine but modest risk premium of approximately 1-2%, reflecting the real volatility of equities.  Second, a structural wealth transfer of approximately 2.5-4%, driven by the asymmetric transmission of monetary expansion through the Cantillon Effect: newly created money enters the financial system first, inflating equity prices while suppressing risk-free rates.  Third, an information distortion of approximately 2-6%, arising from systematically underreported inflation that causes nominal bond yields to be set too low, thereby widening the observed spread between equities and bonds.  We show that governments operating fiat currency systems face powerful, mutually reinforcing incentives to underreport inflation - including the indexation of entitlement spending, the servicing of effectively floating-rate sovereign debt, and the structural interests of a majority-debtor electorate.  Critically, we demonstrate that the asymmetry between equities and bonds is sustained by financial repression: forced buyers of government debt prevent the market from correcting the mispricing.  Together, these three channels fully account for the observed equity premium without requiring implausible risk aversion parameters, exotic preferences, or behavioral anomalies.  The mechanism is not unique to the United States - it is a structural feature of every fiat currency system in the world.

title: The Indo-Pacific and Artificial Intelligence: Legal Challenges and Policy Recommendations
affiliations: University of Macau - Faculty of Law

detail.title: The Indo-Pacific and Artificial Intelligence: Legal Challenges and Policy Recommendations
detail.abstract: Amidst the current global debate on the regulation and governance of artificial intelligence (AI), numerous jurisdictions have already prepared or are drafting regulations to meet the challenges produced by the rise of AI in the global digital economy. In this global race towards the regulation of AI, the Indo-Pacific region has emerged as a potential epicentre of the future global digital economy. For this to happen, however, governments in the region must cooperate and streamline their efforts towards the establishment of a coherent regulatory framework towards various digital technologies. This chapter thus analyses and identifies the main regulatory challenges posed by AI to help formulate some broad recommendations if the region is to tackle the complex problems brought about by the disruptive effects that are inherent in the cross-cutting nature of AI and its related technologies.

title: Decision Compression in Humans and Machines
affiliations: Artificial Intelligence in Finance Institute, Federal Reserve Bank New York and

detail.title: Decision Compression in Humans and Machines
detail.abstract:
Human cognition operates under severe computational constraints, forcing systematic reduction of high-dimensional reality into tractable representations. We formalize this as decisional compression along three orthogonal axes: (i) feature compression, where decisions depend on D = π(X) rather than the full state X ∈ Rn; (ii) target scalarization, where outcome Y is replaced by Z = τ (Y ) such as an expectation or score; and (iii) algorithmic linearization and orthogonalization, where nonlinear interactions are approximated by additive separable models. All three guarantee suboptimality and, in domains like hiring and credit, induce unfairness: individuals whose value lies in compressed-away dimensions or interaction effects are systematically disadvantaged.

We prove each compression type forces irreducible regret and connect them to group conditional risk disparities. We examine manifestations across human resources and finance where credit scores, VaR, and linear factor models compress multidimensional phenomena at substantial cost. AI faces a different trade-off: where humans trade speed for optimality, AI trades interpretability for optimality. Machine-to-machine verification offers a resolution: AI audits AI in full-dimensional space while humans oversee at aggregate level. Yet accepting this resolution requires confronting a prior question: the metrics society already trusts, such as credit scores, Value-at-Risk, and linear factor models, rest on abstractions no more transparent than learned representations; if we already accept theoretically grounded but cognitively opaque compressed metrics for high-stakes decisions, the question is not whether to trust abstract verification but which abstractions to trust.

detail.abstract: Responsible governance increasingly poses a multi-sector, multi-level challenge for managers. It relates to the effective management of a large number of societal interfaces along which companies, government and civil society organizations have to develop distinct means, ways and principles for dealing with sustainability issues. Most sustainability issues supersede the boundaries of the archetypical roles and primary responsibilities of each of the societal spheres (state, market, communities) from which organizations tend to derive primary responsibilities. Hybrid organizational forms are maturing that have taken up these challenges, but these forms face sizable governance challenges as well. The corporate governance discourse consequently requires broadening and nuance at the same time. The agenda for 'responsible governance' should thereby not only deal with traditional corporate governance issuesaimed at correcting improper or irresponsible behaviourbut should also consider how to address wider issues of sustainability, aimed at driving and stimulating positive responsible behaviour. This contribution shows that this challenge requires parallel insights from two angles: a macro and a micro point of view. We construct a societally founded taxonomy of organizational forms and conceptualize four tiers of responsible governance challenges for organizations to delineate an agenda for further research.

title: HayabusaNet: Hybrid attention-based multiscale fusion CNN for accurate and efficient brain tumor classification in MRI scans
affiliations: Kanazawa University, Kanazawa University and Kanazawa University

detail.title: HayabusaNet: Hybrid attention-based multiscale fusion CNN for accurate and efficient brain tumor classification in MRI scans
detail.abstract: ​​Brain tumors are a major clinical threat and are associated with high mortality, making accurate and timely diagnosis from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) essential for treatment planning. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have improved automated MRI analysis. However, many existing models remain computationally expensive and do not fully exploit efficient multiscale feature fusion because they rely on predominantly single-branch, sequential feature extraction. Here, we propose HayabusaNet, a compact CNN that uses depthwise separable convolutions to improve efficiency while preserving discriminative capacity. The network employs parallel multiscale branches with varied kernel sizes and progressively increased channel widths to capture both fine-grained and coarse tumor patterns. We introduce a tailored multiscale feature-fusion scheme to integrate branch outputs, and we incorporate a hybrid attention module to enhance salient local cues while injecting global contextual dependencies. HayabusaNet is evaluated on two public benchmarks: the multiclass Kaggle brain MRI dataset (7,023 images) and the binary Br35H dataset (3,000 images). Model explanations are further examined using Grad-CAM and Grad-CAM++. On the Kaggle dataset, HayabusaNet achieves 98.86% accuracy, 98.84% precision, 98.78% recall, and a 98.81% F1-score. On Br35H, it attains 98.70% for accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. Compared with other deep CNNs, the proposed model improves computational efficiency, as reflected by a lower parameter count and FLOPs, along with faster inference, while maintaining strong classification performance. In conclusion, these results show that combining multiscale feature fusion, efficient convolutions, and hybrid attention can improve the accuracy--efficiency balance for brain MRI classification. The framework also supports interpretation through saliency visualizations.

title: Preferences for Warning Signal Quality: Experimental Evidence
affiliations: University of Oklahoma, University of Arkansas and University of Arkansas, Fayetteville

detail.title: Preferences for Warning Signal Quality: Experimental Evidence
detail.abstract:
We use a laboratory experiment to study preferences over false-positive and false-negative rates of warning signals for an adverse event with a known prior. We find that subjects decrease their demand with signal quality, but less than predicted by our theory. There is asymmetric under-responsiveness by prior: for a low (high) prior, their willingness-to-pay does not fully adjust for the increase in the false-positive (false-negative) costs. We show that neither risk preference nor Bayesian updating skills can fully explain our results. Our results are most consistent with a decision-making heuristic in which subjects do not distinguish between false-positive and false-negative errors.

title: (Stage-Based) Identifying the Effect of War on Inflation

detail.title: (Stage-Based) Identifying the Effect of War on Inflation
detail.abstract: Identifying the causal effect of a macroeconomic shock that affects at the same time an entire country – or the whole world – remains a challenge. Identifying what drives inflation is crucial for guiding central banks’ monetary policy decisions. A big war can potentially impact inflation simultaneously worldwide, and a novel method may help to clearly identify its effect. I apply the Stage-Based Identification method to inflation data from countries in the Eurozone, regions in USA, regions in Brazil, and Länder in Germany to estimate the effect on inflation of Russia invading Ukraine in 2022. The results indicate that, given the state of the world at the time, the war had a positive and economically relevant impact, between 1 and 2 percentage points, on headline inflation in most countries studied. However, in Europe, the sharp inflation spike observed between 2021 and 2022 was only partially explained by this episode.

title: Who Protects the Sheep from the Wolves of Wall Street? A Review of "Fixed" by John Campbell and Tarun Ramadorai (2025)
